notes: Omaha's carrier hotel: a nine-story, ~75,000 sq ft facility with around 8 MW of capacity at 1623 Farnam Street downtown, home to the OmahaIX internet exchange and some 60 carriers. News Press & Gazette Co. subsidiary Berks Group acquired Nebraska Data Centers and the 1623 Farnam carrier hotel in 2018 and established 1623 Farnam LLC, so 'Nebraska Data Centers' as an operator name is historical, not current. Build-out history: a $10 million expansion in 2019 built out the fifth floor, floors six through nine were added in 2021, and the final two data halls completed in June 2025 added 1.5 MW of IT capacity and space for 280 racks. CEO Bill Severn cites 'significant demand from AI workloads, edge deployments, content platforms, and broadband networks'. The company is separately planning an OMA2 campus expansion explicitly aimed at AI and edge infrastructure growth, with no site, size or date disclosed on its own page; it is not listed separately as of August 2026. DCD also reports the facility serves Trump Media & Technology Group; DCD attributes that tenant claim to other reporting, and it is not otherwise recorded. The recorded capacity is the ~8 MW total, not the 1.5 MW increment; no investment figure is recorded, because the only sourced amount is the $10 million 2019 fifth-floor expansion and, as of October 2026, neither cited source gives a total site investment. records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Brownfield redevelopment of former AEP Conesville coal plant (reported as 2,000+ MW by Frontier Group of Companies and as 2,300 MW by its chief operating officer at the October 2025 groundbreaking; operational 62 years, closed May 2020). Frontier Group of Companies acquired the plant in 2020 and built the Conesville Industrial Park across ~2,500 acres; Aligned purchased a 197-acre parcel. Aligned describes the project as 'AI/HPC' and 'Gigascale' in its press materials, and this is its third Ohio campus (others: Perkins Township/Sandusky, 96 MW total; Pataskala). Multi-building campus — renderings show up to four buildings; second, third, and fourth buildings referenced at groundbreaking. As of October 2026, Aligned's press release states no capacity figure; the Coshocton County Port Authority executive director said, as reported by the Athens County Independent, that the final buildout will have a capacity of 340 megawatts. Investment described as 'multi-billion dollar' — as of July 2026, no firm figure was confirmed, so no investment figure is recorded. Aligned's press release says the phased development is anticipated to generate 'thousands of construction jobs and hundreds of high-quality, long-term operational roles'. The Athens County Independent reports the Port Authority executive director saying the project is expected to create more than 1,800 jobs during construction, and Aligned saying it will create 149 jobs in the long term. All are projections. Aligned is exploring on-site nuclear power (SMRs) for this campus and nearby Zanesville/Cambridge sites; no agreement confirmed. Coordinates approximate (village-level). Site infrastructure funding note: the Coshocton Port Authority received a $58.7M grant (Ohio Dept of Development All Ohio Future Fund, announced July 21, 2025) for utility upgrades, water/wastewater extensions, and roadway improvements across the broader industrial park — this benefits Aligned indirectly but is not a direct subsidy to Aligned and is therefore not listed under subsidies.

approval_context.text: Strong positive reception at October 2025 groundbreaking. Coshocton County Commissioners and Port Authority executive director spoke favorably. Site revitalization fills a significant local tax and employment gap left by AEP plant closure (plant formerly provided ~10% of River View Local Schools' annual budget and employed ~600 workers). Broader Ohio policy context: a proposed constitutional amendment that would ban large data centers was under debate at the time of announcement; some community and policy advocates cited this project as evidence of the economic value data centers bring to rural counties.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: No cooling type or water consumption data disclosed. Former coal plant had access to Muskingum River cooling water infrastructure; Aligned has not confirmed whether this will be utilized.

status_history.note: Aligned press release; 197-acre campus at Conesville Industrial Park, foundational customer secured, initial delivery mid-2026
Groundbreaking ceremony held at Conesville Industrial Park

notes: Proposed data center (Marshall Technology & Energy Center, MTEC) plus a co-located natural-gas electric generation facility within Brooks Industrial Park, Marshall. WWMT (2026-04) resolves the load split that earlier reporting left open: up to 1,400 MW required at full buildout, around 1,000 MW of that from on-site gas turbines and up to 400 MW imported from the grid at peak; the 1 GW plant is carried both in the on-site generation figure and as its own power-generation record. ~270 acres (112 buildable), roughly half wetlands. Alterra (Toronto-based) estimates 300-500 direct high-skill jobs. Mayor Wolfersberger (2026-01) called it "just a concept" with "no site plans or utility agreements yet"; due diligence runs into Q3 2026, then construction is "probably 18 months to two years away" if approved. Land is already zoned heavy industrial, so no public referendum is required (unlike Augusta Township). Planned closed-loop liquid cooling. Coordinates are an approximate Marshall-area estimate, not parcel-geocoded; the LDFA purchase price ($1.12M) is for land only, not a project investment figure. In August 2026 the Marshall mayor said Alterra had decided not to build the gas plant, cutting the project's energy use by 60%, and called it "more of an enterprise-class data center now" (WWMT). Planned capacity is left unfilled: the source's ceiling ('up to 1,400 megawatts') describes the initial concept with the gas plant, and as of October 2026 none of the cited sources states a revised figure. Jobs are left unfilled rather than normalized: the source gives a range ('300 to 500 skilled jobs') that does not distinguish construction from permanent. The $1.12M is the land purchase price, not project investment.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. Phase 1: 49MW PG&E grid connection. Potential 50MW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) on-site. Phase 2 adds a second 218,000 sq ft building with alternative backup power solutions. Total planned capacity ~98MW across both phases.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Status updated to under construction: grading permit issued December 11, 2025; building permit issued March 19, 2026; City of Gilroy lists project as Under Construction as of July 2026. Site at 8050 Camino Arroyo in east Gilroy along Hwy 101. Full build-out: 438,000 sq ft across 56 acres. Amazon cites a ~$2 billion investment for the Gilroy project (recorded as the investment figure); its broader Northern California investment of ~$5.1B and ~1,890 jobs since 2009 is regional and not attributable to this site. The 2020 land purchase was $31.3M. Operational job figures conflict and are unconfirmed: the FEIR says employment 'may grow to 50 full-time employees' (a ceiling), the permit application lists 25, and Amazon's promotional materials cite ~90 on-site; the construction workforce is not disclosed.

approval_context.text: Organized resident opposition active. Concerns cited: utility cost spikes, noise, fire and explosion risk from large-scale lithium BESS, and objection to AI use. An appeal was filed July 21, 2025, subsequently withdrawn August 18, 2025. Opponents requested Amazon guarantee the facility would not be used exclusively for AI workloads.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Final EIR-certified use is 23 acre-feet/year total (~7.49 million gallons/yr) at full build-out — 18 AFY for cooling (~0.016 MGD), 3 AFY landscaping, 2 AFY domestic (FEIR p.186); drawn from Gilroy potable supply pending a recycled-water pipeline. Evaporative cooling is triggered only when outdoor temperature exceeds 83F (~3% of the year). Amazon's promotional figure of ~4 million gallons/yr (~36 households) is roughly half the FEIR-certified total and is disputed in a CEQA challenge; Amazon says it aims for 100% reclaimed cooling water by 2030.

notes: One of the two campuses covered by Amazon's $12 billion northwest Louisiana announcement; the other is just north of Blanchard Latex Road in Caddo Parish. KSLA places this campus about five miles north of Benton on the west side of Highway 3. STACK Infrastructure is the developer partner and each campus is approximately 2-3 million sq ft. Program-level figures are deliberately not attributed to this site: the $12 billion investment and the roughly 1,500 construction / 540 permanent job figures cover both campuses jointly, and Amazon's up-to-$400 million public water-infrastructure commitment covers all of its northwest Louisiana campuses. The separately announced Resilient Technology Park campus in west Shreveport is, as of August 2026, tracked as Amazon Web Services Shreveport Campus (Resilient Technology Park); KSLA reported on 2026-02-24 that it is not part of the $12 billion investment. Coordinates are derived from the published road description and are approximate; no parcel coordinate has been published.

approval_context.text: Protesters at the February 2026 announcement raised water-use and environmental concerns about the northwest Louisiana program. Amazon's campuses are expected to become the largest property taxpayer in both Caddo and Bossier parishes. The litigation reported in connection with this program concerned the separate Resilient Technology Park site in west Shreveport, not this campus.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Amazon says it will fund all water and wastewater improvements required by the projects, investing up to $400 million in public water infrastructure across its northwest Louisiana campuses. notes: Conditional use permit application by Atlas Development for about 302 acres across two adjacent parcels at 208 and 329 Stiles Road, a loop road off Euharlee Road. The parcels are owned by Super Land Holdings LLC. According to the county's legal advertisement, if approved the zoning would have gone from A-1 (agricultural) to I-1 (general industrial), with a final decision by Commissioner Steve Taylor on 2026-01-07. The site plan showed seven structures of about 260,000 sq ft each. The Etowah River lies to the west; county Community Development Director Brandon Johnson said the site is directly across the river from Georgia Power's Plant Bowen and that a power easement runs through the property. No capacity or investment figure was disclosed, and no Georgia DRI filing was found for the project. Distinct from Atlas Development's Project Springbank (Barnsley Gardens Road, withdrawn May 2025) and from Project Bunkhouse (Taff Road, a Digital Realty project). Coordinates are the Census geocoder matches for the two stated street addresses (about 160 m apart), not a surveyed site centroid.

approval_context.text: A change.org petition, "Say NO to the Data Center on Euharlee Rd.", started by Dani Hall on 2025-11-17, reached 2,225 signatures. It cited noise, heat, power demand, water use for cooling, diesel generator emissions and habitat loss. At the 2025-11-18 Euharlee City Council meeting, resident Ron Hartman questioned plans for the site; the council took no position. The application was withdrawn on 2025-12-02, before its hearing, and the petition was marked a victory.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: Atlas Development applied for a conditional use permit for a data center on about 302 acres at 208 and 329 Stiles Road, off Euharlee Road; a Bartow County Planning Commission hearing was set for 2025-12-15 (reported 2025-11-14 from the county's legal advertisement).

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Location: off Interstate 530 near 145th Street, Pulaski County; coordinates are approximate for the I-530 corridor south of Little Rock. Named after the Leo constellation. Initial $6B investment may grow to $21B through full build-out. First phase completion targeted June 2027. Campus sits near long-haul fiber routes connecting Dallas, Atlanta, and Memphis. A Q1 2026 construction start was planned as of announcement. As of October 2026, AVAIO's development page says AVAIO "has broken ground" on the campus, while at a July 13, 2026 community meeting AVAIO's project manager said construction was expected to begin in early 2027, with the permits needed to start earthworks in hand (Arkansas Times); the record is listed as proposed. The 760-acre land area is the site size given in the January 2026 announcement and the July 2026 Arkansas Times account; as of October 2026, AVAIO's development page describes a 296-acre project located about 7.7 km from the map pin, which stays approximate. The January 2026 announcement says AVAIO anticipates power demand of up to 1 GW as the facility grows; that is a ceiling on power demand, not IT capacity, so no planned capacity is recorded. The energy source is mixed rather than on-site gas. The 150 MW figure is the Entergy Arkansas grid supply contract, not on-site generation, and as of July 2026 on-site gas capacity was unquantified in sources. The recorded 500 MW of on-site generation is from AVAIO's development page for the campus, which lists "500 MW Total Baseload BTM" (behind the meter) alongside "570 MW Total Grid Power" and "1,070 MW Total Baseload Power"; as of October 2026, the page does not name the fuel for the behind-the-meter capacity. Arkansas's data-center sales-and-use tax exemption (Act 819 of 2023, expanded by Act 548 of 2025) likely applies given the investment scale. AVAIO's development page states that "the State of Arkansas offers substantial Sales and Use Tax incentives for data center tenants, reducing total cost of ownership on qualifying capital expenditures", but as of October 2026 names no award or amount; as of July 2026 no AVAIO-specific incentive award had been published.
capacityMw.planned: Sources give a 150 MW Entergy Arkansas supply contract and a ceiling of up to 1 GW of anticipated power demand, but no IT capacity; neither figure is a planned capacity.

approval_context.text: Pulaski County adopted a one-year data-center moratorium (10 votes) in May 2026 but exempted AVAIO by a bare 8-vote majority — the minimum on the 15-member Quorum Court. Residents opposed the project over water use and farmland; it is backed by state and county leadership and the Little Rock Regional Chamber.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: AVAIO's project manager testified to the Pulaski County Quorum Court that the campus would demand about 200,000 gallons of water per day on average during warmer months, dropping to near zero in winter; as of July 6, 2026, the specific cooling technology had not been disclosed. At a community meeting in Wrightsville on July 13, 2026, AVAIO said it planned a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates water and would consume 8,000 gallons a day of potable water from Central Arkansas Water, with 4,000 gallons a day discharged into the 145th Street Sewer District (Arkansas Times). Both figures are company projections; the campus is not yet operating.

status_history.note: AVAIO Digital announces $6B+ AI-ready data center campus in Pulaski County; Governor Sanders describes it as largest economic investment in Arkansas history; construction targeted Q1 2026 start

The record is listed as permitted, not proposed: the project holds a CEC opt-in certification (99 MW, Dec 8 2025) and a City of Pittsburg Commercial Design Review approval (Dec 11 2025, modified Feb 12 2026); no source confirms groundbreaking/construction has started. The planned capacity of 99 MW reflects the CEC-certified figure. AVAIO's December 2025 release says the Pittsburg Technology Park Specific Plan "allows AVAIO to develop up to 500MW"; that is a ceiling the plan permits, not a planned capacity, so it is not recorded. The AI classification is recorded as likely: AVAIO's own materials use explicit 'AI and cloud-driven deployments' language but do not publish GPU/HPC-specific technical specs. The Center for Biological Diversity's CEQA lawsuit (Case No. N24-2162, filed Dec 2024) was settled in Dec 2025 (CBD agreed not to oppose Phase 1 in exchange for 100% renewable/carbon-free electricity, rooftop solar, 100% recycled water for cooling, wildlife monitoring, and a $750,000 community climate-resiliency payment) - it is not an active legal threat, though broader public opposition continues (see community).

notes: Distinct from AVAIO's 'Leo' campus in Little Rock/Pulaski County AR — do not conflate. Site: East Metropolitan Center Business and Industrial Park, Brandon. Land acreage: AVAIO's own project page and groundbreaking materials cite 329 acres; the August 19 press release cited 175 acres — 329 used as more authoritative per operator's site. Capacity: 116 MW initial via executed ESA with Entergy Mississippi (energized June 2027 per operator site); Entergy guiding an additional 420 MW of grid power available by end of 2030; access to Gulf South Pipeline for up to 500 MW of on-site behind-the-meter thermal generation starting Q2 2027 — total baseload path to over 1 GW. The 116 MW planned figure reflects the executed first-phase ESA only; full buildout remains a projection. Investment: $6B stated without 'up to' qualifier across operator, MDA, and Governor's office sources; Governor's office describes it as the third-largest economic development project in Mississippi history. Jobs: 'at least 60 direct, high-tech jobs' and 'hundreds of indirect jobs ranging from construction to other related industries' — projections, not firm figures; no construction vs permanent breakdown confirmed. Rooftop solar of 20+ MW planned (behind-the-meter). Recycled water and new sewer line extension cited by operator as water infrastructure options. Estimated $23M in ad valorem tax revenue annually per Rankin First (county economic development group). Coordinates approximate (Brandon city center, Rankin County).

approval_context.text: Strong official support: Governor Reeves, Mayor Butch Lee (Brandon), Rankin County, and MDA all endorsed project. Community opposition emerged before groundbreaking: online petition to Rankin County Board of Supervisors demanded written guarantees against utility bill increases and air/water pollution, and called for construction halt if guarantees cannot be made. Residents cited concerns about water consumption, air pollution (referencing xAI Memphis gas turbine precedent), power demands, and traffic. Community group 'Mississippi For Mississippi' produced an impact-distance map. Rankin County supervisors did not respond to press inquiries. No litigation reported.

notes: Very early-stage: AWS states no formal proposal submitted as of DCD article date. Site plan application filed May 2026. Concept design shared at community open house shows up to 8 buildings south and west of Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant. Capacity not disclosed by AWS. Coordinates approximate for Calvert Cliffs area.

approval_context.text: Calvert County commissioners rejected a proposed 24-month moratorium on data center approvals at April 7, 2026 meeting (3 voted no, 2 voted yes). County zoning ordinance effective approximately March 2025 defines data center use standards for heavy industrial zones including setbacks, design, and noise requirements.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: AWS held community open house; described project as 'preliminary review work, regulatory analysis, site evaluation and early design concepts.' Site plan application filed May 4, 2026 with fees paid May 18. Up to 8 data centers proposed. No rezoning required (already heavy industry zoning).

Amazon Data Services Inc. formally withdrew its Calvert Technology Center Conceptual Site Development Plan application and decided not to pursue the proposed data center project in Calvert County. Calvert County Government announced the withdrawal in an Aug. 4, 2026 press release; the county's data center page now records the application as withdrawn and states no site plan applications for data center development are pending. The withdrawal followed voter backlash in the county's June 23, 2026 primary, and the county subsequently passed a six-month moratorium on data center site plan approvals effective Aug. 28, 2026.

notes: Hinds County site, distinct from the aggregate record AWS Project Atlas – Madison County Mega Site (Canton), whose own notes name only the two Madison County complexes (Madison County Mega Site near Canton and the Costas Property in Ridgeland) and cite the Hinds County $1B figure only as part of Amazon's $25B statewide total — as of September 2026 it was not otherwise recorded as a facility. Site is the long-vacant former Delphi auto-parts plant in the Clinton Industrial Park, mostly empty since 2009; AWS describes it as the first time it has retrofitted an existing industrial building into a data center at this scale. Coordinates are a geocode of Clinton, MS (city centroid), not of the site; WLBT gives the street address as 1001 Industrial Park Dr., and as of September 2026 no source found gave the industrial-park parcel. As of September 2026, no source found states IT capacity in MW or acreage. WLBT describes the building as a 690,000 square foot facility; an earlier WLBT report gives the structure as 730,000 square feet, according to LoopNet. The Fee-in-Lieu of Taxes agreement, approved by the Clinton Board of Aldermen and the Hinds County Board of Supervisors at special meetings on January 15, 2026, is recorded from WLBT's account of its terms. As of September 2026, no source found gave a dollar value for it: WLBT reports that the city attorney was unaware of a dollar amount, and the City of Clinton page states only that the investment will 'generate millions of dollars in new revenue'. The record is listed as under construction rather than operational: a ribbon-cutting was held 2026-06-12 but Entergy's account describes the project as under development and not yet operational, and a separate groundbreaking was also reported — the sources conflict on whether it has begun serving traffic. Water/cooling: as of September 2026, no source was found for reporting that the Clinton building will not use water. Mississippi Today, republished by DeSoto County News, reports Amazon saying the facility will have a minimal water footprint because it will be air-cooled, using air-cooled chillers, and the water notes record that.
records.water_notes: Amazon describes this site as having a minimal water footprint and being cooled exclusively by air-cooled chillers, a design constraint of retrofitting the existing building. Recorded as closed-loop rather than air-cooled under the project's tie-breaker rule: an air-cooled chiller plant still runs a recirculating water/coolant circuit, and the air-cooled type is reserved for designs with no cooling water circuit at all.

status_history.note: Ribbon-cutting held in Clinton marking Amazon's $1 billion investment converting the former Delphi manufacturing plant into a data center; Entergy's account describes the project as under development rather than in service.

records.segment_basis: Hyperscale / cloud operator classification from the reported operator. Building scale and workload are not inferred.
records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Independent evidence indicates Canton and Ridgeland are two distinct AWS campuses, not a single project under two names. Mississippi Free Press (2026-08-19), reporting Madison County's denial of AWS's tax-valuation appeal, states directly: 'The county has entered into two fee-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements with the tech giant for its data center campuses in Canton and Ridgeland' -- i.e., Madison County's own tax/incentive administration treats these as two separate FILOT agreements, not one. Magnolia Tribune (2024-07-24) gives the physical distinction: the Madison County Mega Site is '927 acres ... located off Highway 22 and Nissan Parkway in Canton,' while the Costas Property is 'an additional 786 acres in Ridgeland ... located along the southern tip of Madison County near Tougaloo College, on the corner of Highland Colony Parkway and West County Line Road' -- roughly 20 miles apart. Both sites are within Madison County (Ridgeland is not a separate county), so the 'Madison County' framing of the aggregate record AWS Project Atlas – Madison County Mega Site (Canton) is not wrong on that count, but as of September 2026 it combined two separately-incentivized campuses. Coordinates are the OSM-tagged traffic-signal node at the actual Highland Colony Parkway / West County Line Road intersection (confirmed against current OpenStreetMap data, not an estimate), not a confirmed parcel boundary -- an approximate pin. Capacity, investment and jobs are not recorded, because every figure found for this project (the $10B investment, the combined MW target, job counts) is stated for the two-site project as a whole; no cited source apportions any of these by site, and apportioning by acreage share would be a fabricated estimate, not a sourced fact.

approval_context.text: As of September 2026, no Ridgeland-specific community reaction is reported in the cited sources; the aggregate record documents Canton-side (dust/noise/air-quality) opposition, which this record does not duplicate absent Ridgeland-specific evidence.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: Reported as 'in the early stages of construction'; both Madison County sites estimated for completion by 2027.

notes: Two distinct complexes: Madison County Mega Site (outside Canton) and Costas Property (west of Tougaloo College near County Line Rd, Ridgeland). Amazon's total Mississippi statewide commitment expanded to $25B including subsequent Warren County ($3B) and Hinds County ($1B) announcements. Coordinates are approximate Canton-area centroid. The Veolia water partnership claim was removed: the About Amazon source names Arable (not Veolia) as water replenishment partner; recycled wastewater target of 83M gallons/year by 2027 is confirmed. Narrowed to Canton on 2026-09-10 (maintainer adjudication): this record previously combined two campuses. Madison County's own tax administration treats them as separate — it 'has entered into two fee-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements with the tech giant for its data center campuses in Canton and Ridgeland' (Mississippi Free Press, 2026-08-19) — and Magnolia Tribune (2024-07-24) gives the physical split: the Madison County Mega Site is '927 acres ... located off Highway 22 and Nissan Parkway in Canton', while the Costas Property is 'an additional 786 acres in Ridgeland'. The Ridgeland campus is therefore, as of September 2026, tracked separately as AWS Costas Property Campus (Ridgeland), and the land acreage here was reduced from the combined 1,700 to Canton's 927 so the two records do not double-count acreage. The capacity, investment and jobs figures on this record remain program-level figures from the original Project Atlas announcement covering both Madison County campuses; they are left in place here rather than split, because no source apportions them per campus. They should not be summed with AWS Costas Property Campus (Ridgeland), which carries no capacity, investment or jobs figures for this reason. The location was also corrected from an exact pin to an approximate pin: this record's notes already stated the coordinate is a Canton-area centroid, so the exact-pin claim was wrong. The two campuses are treated by Madison County's tax and incentive administration as legally and financially separate: the Madison County Mega Site (927 acres, off Highway 22 and Nissan Parkway, Canton) and the Costas Property (786 acres, Highland Colony Parkway / West County Line Road, Ridgeland), as confirmed by a 2026-08-19 Mississippi Free Press report on Madison County's denial of AWS's Canton tax-valuation appeal: the county 'has entered into two fee-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements with the tech giant for its data center campuses in Canton and Ridgeland.' The latitude and longitude (32.6121, -90.039) read as Canton-specific, closer to Canton than to Ridgeland. The combined capacity (1000 MW planned), investment ($10B) and jobs (7,000/1,000) are not apportioned by site: as of September 2026, no source found states a per-site breakdown, and apportioning by acreage share (54%/46%) would be a fabricated estimate. Ridgeland is itself within Madison County, so the aggregate's 'Madison County' framing is not geographically wrong, only combined.

approval_context.text: Canton neighbors report dust, noise and air-quality effects and say they were not consulted; the Southern Environmental Law Center has raised ambient-air-standard concerns over the 700+ diesel generators. No litigation over the Canton campus is documented in the fetched sources.

notes: Codename 'Project Green'; application filed via NorthPoint Development, LLC. Two-phase build-out: Phase 1 = 8 data center buildings; Phase 2 = 13 additional buildings (21 total). Located on ~1,000 acres at northeast quadrant of I-70 and Highway 19 interchange near New Florence. Official AWS/Governor Kehoe announcement on June 15, 2026 cited a $10B investment commitment. Earlier county planning documents and initial filings referenced a maximum capital investment ceiling of up to $35B — that figure is a speculative ceiling, not a committed amount. AWS separately announced a 138MW renewable energy project in Missouri; not confirmed as dedicated to this campus. Community investments included in announcement: $3M for county 911/emergency dispatch upgrades, $3M for community programs, $1M for Montgomery County Fairgrounds, $150K community fund, $50K teacher grant. Preserve Montgomery County LLC filed suit in February 2026 alleging ten counts of Missouri Sunshine Law violations (closed-session negotiations, NDAs with Amazon); case pending as of mid-2026. First buildings targeted operational by 2027; full campus potentially complete ~2032. Coordinates are approximate (parcel centroid at I-70 / Hwy 19 NE quadrant). Jobs: KOMU reported ~400 permanent jobs; DCD's coverage of the same $10B announcement cited no specific permanent figure (only 'thousands of construction jobs') — permanent count left unstructured pending firm corroboration.

approval_context.text: Preserve Montgomery County LLC (coalition of local residents, farmers, and business owners) filed a 10-count lawsuit in February 2026 alleging Missouri Sunshine Law violations — specifically that county commissioners conducted negotiations in closed sessions and signed NDAs with Amazon. Community concerns at public meetings included water usage impacts, potential electric rate increases, and loss of rural character. Some residents and officials expressed support for the project's economic benefits. Construction proceeded despite the pending suit. Montgomery County Commission stated real property taxes are not abated and projected the project would double the county's tax revenue at full buildout.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Water sourced from Cambrian-Ordovician aquifer via wells drilled to ~1,500 ft depth (to avoid impacting local private wells at shallower depths). Initial phase projected at 2.9M gallons/year; full 17-building campus projected at ~50M gallons/year (~0.137 MGD equivalent). Regional aquifer capacity exceeds 23 trillion gallons; current regional utilization ~8%; this project adds ~0.03%. On-site stormwater management ponds and water treatment plant planned. Cooling methodology not publicly specified.

status_history.note: Application filed via NorthPoint Development, LLC for a 1,000-acre parcel at the northeast quadrant of I-70 and Highway 19 interchange near New Florence; two-phase campus of up to 21 data center buildings.

Montgomery County Commission unanimously approved the project and tax abatement incentive framework in December 2025; public safety entities (ambulance district, fire protection district) opted out of Chapter 100 participation and retained full tax allocations.

notes: ~$4.8B campus near Wallula, Walla Walla County; operator reported (not officially confirmed) to be AWS, so the record was marked reported. Coordinates are the Wallula area centroid. Operator confirmed as Amazon Data Services when the Port of Walla Walla amended the buyer from Advance Phase LLC to Amazon Data Services (Feb 12, 2026 commission vote; >550 acres for >$36M land) — the record was then marked confirmed. The reported ~$4.8B (DCD) / ~$5B (local) campus figure is an estimate across ~4 phases, not a firm pledge, so no investment figure is recorded. Port projects ~720 direct+indirect jobs at full build-out of its four-phase, 16-building concept (projection), so no jobs figure is recorded; Amazon's FAQ for the three-building application projects 120-150 full-time positions. The application before Walla Walla County (the Amazon Attalia Data Center Campus) covers three buildings of about 220,000 sq ft each on a 134-acre parcel, smaller than the Port's concept, so the land area recorded is that parcel. As of October 2026 no cited source states a capacity figure for the campus, so no planned capacity is recorded. Eligible for Washington's rural-county server-equipment sales/use-tax exemption (RCW 82.08.986) but no DOR certificate is confirmed, so no subsidy is recorded. Amazon's August 2026 community materials describe the cooling as outside air about 93% of the year, with water-based cooling (water-soaked pads) for about 7%, and give the cooling-water source as a new non-potable Columbia River supply system being developed with the Port of Walla Walla, with potable groundwater from the utility as temporary cooling water for about a year while that system is built.
capacityMw.planned: As of October 2026, no cited source states a planned capacity for this campus.

approval_context.text: Port of Walla Walla commissioners approved the amended land sale unanimously (Feb 12, 2026), calling the project transformative; documented concerns from the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation (sacred Snake/Columbia confluence), environmental and academic voices, and a commissioner over water and power. No litigation or moratorium; a SEPA environmental review with tribal and public comment is still pending.

approval_context.text: More than 23,000 petition signatures collected (Nature Forward, July 2026). County Executive Aisha Braveboy issued executive order in September 2025 pausing development. WTOP quotes a council member pointing to "the data center project proposed for the old Landover Mall site, which the county is trying to stop, as one she considered harmful" -- i.e. this site. Nature Forward (July 30, 2026) reports that the council's two-year moratorium covers new applications for preliminary subdivision plans and detailed site plans, and does not block this project, whose preliminary plan was approved in 2024 and which is exempt from detailed site plan review. Qualified Data Center Task Force created. Predominantly Black community (63% African American census tract); environmental justice concerns raised.

notes: Master-planned data center park on a ~2,069-acre former residential (Cipriani) parcel Tract acquired for ~$136M, south of I-10 in Buckeye; planned for up to ~20M sq ft across as many as 40 data centers at full build-out over ~15 years (~$20B). Coordinates are an approximate town-level geocode (Buckeye, south of I-10), not a parcel-confirmed point. The City of Buckeye executed a development agreement with AZLCO Buckeye, LLC (Ordinance No. 08-24, adopted unanimously 2024-08-06). It reimburses the developer for six enumerated regional infrastructure components it builds and dedicates to the city — two public-safety sites, temporary and permanent public-safety facilities, $15M toward the Johnson Road interchange, and oversized regional water infrastructure — funded by 20% of the tax revenue the project itself generates, beginning only after the city has received $60M cumulatively and terminating 20 years from the effective date. It is capped at "the lesser of" the developer's verified costs or $50,000,000, so it cannot exceed what the developer actually spent; it is cost recovery for public infrastructure rather than an incentive, abatement or credit, and is therefore not recorded as a subsidy. Nothing has been paid to date. Buckeye's economic-development director has projected "more than 360 jobs at full build out" — an end-state across as many as 40 separate future data centers, none yet leased, permitted or built, and so not recorded as a permanent-jobs figure for this site. A search of 226 Buckeye Council and P&Z agendas (Feb 2024 – Aug 2026) found no GPLET and no Foreign Trade Zone instrument.

approval_context.text: Buckeye City Council approved a development agreement granting Tract up to $50M in public infrastructure reimbursements; the mayor voiced strong support and no organized opposition is documented across multiple independent press accounts.

notes: The address '902 East Leith Street, Flint, MI' for the broader former Buick City complex is independently confirmed by two sources: Genesee County View's 2023-05-25 piece on Ashley Capital's adjacent 'Flint Commerce Center' redevelopment ('The site address provided in the article is: 902 E. Leith St. in Flint'), and EPA's own 2023-11-01 press release on the Flint Commerce Center LLC prospective-purchaser agreement for 'roughly 330 acres of the former Buick City manufacturing facility.' Leith Street is independently documented (via a non-cited Wikipedia cross-check, used only to sanity-check geography, not as a source) as the street that divides the ~413-acre Buick City site into northern and southern sections, and the chosen Leith Street road segment (of several OpenStreetMap-tagged segments) falls within the site's other documented boundary streets (E Pierson Rd to the north, N Saginaw St/Industrial to the west, E Hamilton Ave to the south, James P Cole Blvd to the east -- all geocoded to confirm the bounding box). This is the general Buick City site address, NOT a confirmed parcel boundary for Hillwood-Sterling's specific ~200-acre sub-parcel within it (Ashley Capital, not Hillwood-Sterling, is RACER Trust's direct purchaser of the larger site; Hillwood-Sterling's deal, per Gander Newsroom, is reported as a ~200-acre interest within the broader former Buick City footprint) -- the approximate pin reflects both the geocode-not-parcel caveat AND this sub-parcel uncertainty. The record is marked reported, not rumored: Gander Newsroom (updated 2026-09-03) names a specific developer ('Hillwood-Sterling, a joint venture backed by Dallas-based real estate developer Ross Perot Jr.') and a specific acreage under contract, which is more than an unsourced rumor, though it still falls short of a permit or filed site plan -- as of September 2026, none exists yet because the moratorium blocks the city from accepting one. The record is listed as proposed: Gander Newsroom states 'it's still unclear who the end user would be for a potential Flint project -- or what size and investment it would involve,' and the moratorium (in effect since 2026-06-08) means 'no permit applications, site plans, or construction for data centers will be accepted or processed by the city of Flint' -- so, as of September 2026, no site-plan or rezoning application can exist yet by design, not by omission. No megawatt capacity, investment figure, or job count appears in any source consulted.

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Developer's campus page states verbatim: "A 95 acre development out of a 650 acre lot" with "less than 15% of the site planned for development"; "$6 billion"; two data center buildings plus supporting infrastructure; "2027 First Building Completed"; currently in a "planning, engineering, and community engagement phase"; "up to 1,000 construction workers at peak construction" and "250 staff for operations" at an "average salary of $115,000". The recorded land area is the 650-acre site; the built footprint is 95 acres. No capacity is recorded: the campus page states no MW figure. Secondary coverage attributes 6 GW to Beacon's whole portfolio of six-plus campuses across Alberta, New Brunswick, Tom Green County TX, Kern County CA and Calvert; that is a portfolio figure, not this site's capacity, and is not recorded. County ambiguity: Beacon's own page places the hub in Mobile County and that is what is recorded, but Calvert is an unincorporated community straddling Mobile and Washington counties, and the OSM village node used for the coordinate sits on the Washington County side. As of September 2026, the county had not been confirmed against the parcel. Subsidy: no incentive or abatement is mentioned on the developer's page; Mobile County and Alabama Commerce records had not been checked as of September 2026, so this is an unchecked gap, not an audited negative. Coordinates are the Calvert community centroid, not the 650-acre parcel.

approval_context.text: Beacon held a community open house on June 17, 2026 attended by more than 50 residents; the project is drawing questions from some nearby residents about land use, utilities and long-term impact on the rural community, without organised opposition reported in this coverage.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Developer states verbatim: "The site will utilize a closed-loop water system. Evaporative cooling will not be used." That is an explicit recirculating circuit with evaporative rejection ruled out — a closed-loop cooling type, not air (a water circuit exists) and not evaporative. The developer's campus page says South Alabama Utilities has confirmed availability of 7,500 gallons of public water use and 7,500 gallons of sewer use per day, an allocation intended primarily for employee facilities, and that the project will use approximately 7,500 gallons of water and sewer per day, roughly comparable to a small office building with 250 employees. That is a stated allocation and projection for a proposed campus, not measured use, so no water-use figure is recorded.

Deca projects roughly $40 million a year in local tax revenue by 2034 ($33M to Carroll County Schools, the balance to the county, library, health department and extension services). The project's own site describes phases 1–3 (site selection, evaluation, power) as complete and phase 4 (permitting/engagement) in progress. No capacity figure has been published. Construction-jobs figures differ slightly between sources (7,400 in the Carroll News-Democrat, 'more than 7,000' in Louisville Business First); the more specific figure is recorded. status_history.note: Carroll County Fiscal Court approved and signed a letter to the Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority supporting Deca's application for state tax incentives; the letter was described as neither approving nor disapproving the project itself.

records.name: Carrollton Industrial Campus
records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. Louisville Public Media reports that the campus would "reportedly use 800 megawatts" and names no utility. As of October 2026, no cited source describes an agreement to purchase 800 MW from Kentucky Utilities. Louisville Business First (via Yahoo News) says the project team has conducted power studies to ensure available capacity from Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, and the first cited article says it is unclear how much electricity the data center will need and that developers said studies show LG&E has the capacity to serve the facility. One report puts the land under purchase option at 550 acres south of Carrollton near the Kentucky River and says about 300 acres would carry the data center campus, with the balance reserved for landscaping, setbacks and buffers.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Developers (Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, the same partnership behind PowerHouse Data Centers – Louisville (Camp Ground Road), tracked separately as of September 2026) have secured purchase options and completed initial site studies but had not started construction as of the 2026-09-10 source check; 'it's unclear when construction ... will begin.' Data center footprint is reported as roughly 300 acres. WHAS11 describes a 500-acre site that includes 342 acres owned by Carrollton Utilities, adjacent to its regional wastewater treatment plant; another report puts the land under purchase option at 550 acres, and a third describes the mayor's July 2025 option contract as covering 340 acres of public land. The recorded land area uses the 500-acre figure. An economic-impact analysis projects about $93.2M in local tax revenue (Louisville Business First calls it annual), over $64M of it to Carroll County Public Schools; the developer also received $3.7 million in Kentucky Business Investment (KBI) incentive funding (year not stated in source, so it is not recorded as a subsidy).

approval_context.text: Carroll County/Ghent-area residents organized opposition (group 'No Data Center 502') after learning the Carrollton Industrial Campus had reportedly been in development for over a year before its public announcement. Reporting says the Carrollton mayor signed an unrecorded real estate option contract in July 2025 to sell 340 acres of public land for the project. Residents cite lack of transparency: 'There's been no transparency from our local government' (Laura Beth Austin); 'I don't trust the jobs numbers. I don't trust the tax numbers' (Amy Wright). State Sen. Gex Williams (R) said the city 'made some serious mistakes in terms of their NDAs'; Sen. Keturah Herron (D) said 'If you are not being open and honest ... then we can only assume that it's shady business happening.' A Kentucky State Senate District 20 candidate (Stella Pollard) and the Louisville group opposing a separate PowerHouse/Poe project have joined the organizing.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: $2.5B, ~1.5 million sq ft across three two-story hyperscale buildings (each >80 MW) on a 49.7-acre site; ComEd grid partnership. Update: the village board approved a revised plan (~Oct 2025) consolidating the original three two-story buildings into two three-story buildings plus a second electrical substation, superseding the building-count description above; confirmed delivery targets are the first building in 2027 and the second by end of 2030. As of July 2026, CloudHQ was mid-permitting the revised design (~3,700 drawing sheets, 1,500+ pages of structural calcs); the village hired outside firm HR Green to review it. Construction is active, with cranes on the fenced 50-acre site as of January 2026. Public reception, as of 2026-09-10: the Daily Herald's Mount Prospect coverage and the original CloudHQ groundbreaking press release could not be read past a paywall or block. Notable circumstantial signal: the Village of Mount Prospect maintains its own dedicated 'Community Information and Fact Check Portal' page specifically for this project, which typically indicates the village has been fielding enough resident questions/concerns to warrant an official FAQ/rebuttal page -- but that page's content could not be read either, so no public-reception status is asserted from an inference that could not be verified. Search results also point to reporting, not read directly, that Illinois data-center opposition broadly 'escalates' statewide and that the village sought outside help on Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)-related permitting questions; neither could be confirmed as specific to community opposition at this site. Public reception is therefore given as unknown rather than guessed.

status_history.note: Groundbreaking with ComEd on hyperscale campus

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: 450-acre, two-phase project (Phase 1: 240 acres, reportedly 270-300 MW across three to six buildings - sources disagree on the building count; Phase 2: 210 acres, up to roughly 600 MW combined) near the Fillmore Street and Avenue 52 intersection in eastern Coachella. The record is listed as cancelled as the closest available status: the city's only concrete agreement with the developer was terminated by City Council on 2026-06-04 and the city is one to two votes (2026-08-12, 2026-08-26) from a permanent data-center ban, though the developer has not formally withdrawn. As of August 2026, no AI/HPC-specific marketing was found anywhere - both the developer and press use generic 'data center'/'technology campus' language; the NBC headline's 'AI data center' phrasing is journalistic shorthand, not developer marketing. Planned around three microgrids and an energy center under a self-supplied municipal-utility model (Coachella Valley Power Services LLC, a Stronghold subsidiary; DMK Project Solutions Services is the named project-management partner); the Imperial Irrigation District separately projected approximately $42M in municipal-utility infrastructure financing - not project capex, so no investment figure is recorded. The recorded planned capacity of 270 MW is the Phase 1 total that Stronghold Power Systems states (three buildings at a rated 90 MW each, per Patch) and does not include Phase 2; GPS Business Insider gives a minimum of 270 MW of capacity and up to 300 MW of electricity demand for Phase 1. As of August 2026, jobs are disclosed only as vague estimates ('hundreds of local jobs'), so no jobs figure is recorded. Only cross-streets are known (Fillmore Street and Avenue 52) - no parcel address confirmed. Coordinates are an approximate road-segment geocode (Avenue 52), not a parcel-confirmed point.

approval_context.text: Hundreds attended town halls over water use, power costs, air quality, noise, farmland loss, and proximity to Valle del Sol Elementary (about 2 miles). Former Mayor Steven Hernandez, a recipient of Stronghold campaign donations, pleaded guilty to a felony conflict-of-interest charge in 2026. As of August 2026, no lawsuit was found (unlike the already-tracked IVCM facility in Imperial County). Neighboring Indio is independently pursuing its own data-center ban as part of a regional trend.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: Coachella City Council approved a conceptual Municipal Utility Development Agreement with Coachella Valley Power Services LLC, a Stronghold Power Systems subsidiary; the project never reached the Planning Commission for its own land-use entitlements.

City Council unanimously terminated the Stronghold utility agreement and approved a 45-day data-center moratorium after sustained community opposition. The moratorium was extended roughly 10.5 months on 2026-07-08, and the Planning Commission recommended a permanent citywide data-center ban (two conditions attached) on 2026-07-15, with Council adoption votes scheduled for 2026-08-12 and 2026-08-26.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. About 35 on-site natural-gas turbines (a combined 422 MW per SELC and aerial imagery) supplement a 150 MW grid substation and Tesla Megapack storage. The Shelby County Health Department permitted only 15 turbines; the SELC/NAACP/Young, Gifted & Green appeal of that permit was dismissed as moot by the Memphis and Shelby County Air Pollution Control Board on a 6-1 vote on 2025-12-15 (after the health department and xAI argued most turbines had been removed), ending the appeal-triggered stay and leaving the permit in force; press at the time reported 12 SCR-equipped turbines still active and a permit expiring 2027-01-02. TVA's board voted unanimously on 2026-02-11 to approve an additional 150 MW of firm power, which would double the approved grid allocation to about 300 MW; that approval is contingent on contractual, financial and operational requirements and is a ceiling, not delivered power — as of 2026-09-23 no source reports the second increment energized, and the site is still described as taking 150 MW from the grid. xAI said the Phase-I temporary turbines would be demobilized after grid connection, but 2025 aerial imagery shows 35 on site.

Miss.) targets xAI's separate 'Colossus Gas Plant' in Southaven, Mississippi (MZX Tech LLC, 2875 Stanton Road South), not this site or CTC Property LLC; it cites this site's turbine history only as background. The permit drew 1,700+ public comments, most opposed, and South Memphis (Boxtown) residents already face elevated asthma and cancer rates. xAI did not pursue a Shelby County EDGE PILOT tax abatement; no public subsidy is on record.

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Conditionally selected, currently in exclusive negotiations with the US Army (not finalized); expected completion ~2029. Would be CyrusOne's first Utah facility, developed in partnership with Carlyle. Framed as AI-driven Army infrastructure ('AI is a strategic asset... force multiplier' per the Army Secretary) rather than marketed as a standalone AI-brand product. Coordinates are approximate. In exclusive negotiations with the US Army as of the cited source. Subsidies checked at the municipal tier (2026-09-05): no site-level subsidy found. — structural, not merely unresearched: Dugway Proving Ground is U.S. Army-owned federal land in unincorporated Tooele County, which sits outside any county/municipal property-tax roll, so a Title 17C Community Reinvestment Agency increment or abatement is not possible here regardless of county policy. Any public-sector instrument would be a federal Army real-estate arrangement, not a local or state subsidy, and the site remains in exclusive negotiations, not a finalized agreement. Utah's EDTIF programme excludes data centres and the UCA 59-12-104 exemption is self-executing.

notes: Subsidies checked at the municipal tier (2026-09-05): no site-level subsidy found. Bluffdale's RDA runs three project areas — Gateway Redevelopment Area and Eastern Bluffdale EDA on the Redwood Road/Bangerter Highway corridor, and Jordan Crossing CRA along the Jordan River near the Utah County border — and DataBank's Granite Point campus on Pony Express Road falls outside all three by street-corridor and section/township/range legal-description cross-reference, not a parcel-level GIS overlay. The Jordan Crossing CRA's own draft plan names four illustrative development sites and none is Granite Point, DataBank, or Pony Express Road; no RDA board minutes or agenda mentions either. DataBank's own marketing blog names only the statewide sales-tax exemption on data-center equipment as an incentive for its Salt Lake-area sites — an entity-level, self-executing state exemption, not a Bluffdale-specific award. Utah's EDTIF programme excludes data centres and the UCA 59-12-104 exemption is self-executing.

records.name: Digi Power X Columbiana AI Data Center
records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.

power.scope: facility / project; source scope requires verification
power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. "Digi Power X has an agreement with Alabama Power for the facility and plans to build out in two phases, with Phase 1 comprising 15 megawatts of information technology load and Phase 2 delivering 25 MW for a combined total of 40 MW." The article adds that "The property already supported 22 MW through a substation that was left over from the operation of the Grede Foundry."

notes: Subsidy: the Columbiana City Council "unanimously rejected a tax abatement proposal for Digi Power X", and the article states "The only governmental body that has the jurisdiction to give an abatement on taxes for the Columbiana data center is the City Council." So as of 29 May 2026 this site had no local tax abatement, and by the reporter's account no other body could have granted one. Digi Power X had requested abatement on "all state and local non-educational property taxes on the project's industrial development property" plus construction-related transaction taxes through 2027. WBRC reported on 24 July 2026 that the council had later voted to grant DigiPowerX "a 12-month sales and use tax abatement, but only during construction to help cover the cost of equipment for expansion", in return for a $3.5 million "community impact payment" to the city. Anchor tenant: 10-year master services agreement with Cerebras Systems for colocation of the 40 MW AI data center, "valued at approximately $1.1 billion with potential for the contract value to reach $2.5 billion, inclusive of renewal terms" — that $1.1B is contract value, not capital investment, and is not recorded as the investment figure; the $371.5M figure is the stated "total investment ... in building, machinery and personal property" from the abatement filing. Bham Now (June 2026) instead reports a 55 MW two-phase plan, with 22 MW and $176 million for the first phase and $440 million in total; those figures differ from the 40 MW colocation agreement and the abatement-filing figure and are not recorded. Jobs: "Digi Power X plans to start out with two jobs at a total annual payroll of $200,000 and to expand to 45 permanent jobs by year three with a total payroll of $4.5 million" — the 2 is the year-one headcount, not a construction workforce, so no construction job count is recorded; the source states no construction-worker count. Site history: property purchased by Digihost Technology Inc from Grede II LLC on 21 June 2022 after the Grede Foundry closed in 2020, and run as a bitcoin-mining operation until the January 2025 conversion announcement. Air emissions to be monitored by ADEM. Coordinates are the OSM industrial-park polygon centroid for Industrial Parkway, not a confirmed parcel footprint.

approval_context.text: "Since its announcement, residents have expressed disapproval for the data center leading to a town hall in January 2026 that answered questions regarding the facility. In February, the Columbiana City Council approved an ordinance placing restrictions on any future data centers." The City Council then "unanimously rejected a tax abatement proposal for Digi Power X" following the 5 May 2026 Cerebras announcement.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: The abatement filing states only that "the site will utilize water for liquid cooling" and that noise will come from cooling equipment. The source does not state whether the water circuit recirculates or how heat is rejected, so the cooling type is deliberately left unknown rather than guessed.

status_history.note: Digihost/Digi Power X announced the former Grede Foundry site, in use as a bitcoin-mining operation since 2022, would be converted to a data center.

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
notes: DigiCo Infrastructure REIT is externally managed by HMC Capital (ASX-listed); the applicant/signing entity was HMC StratCap 1977 Saturn, LLC. Approximately 250,000 sq ft hyperscale data center campus planned at 1977 Saturn Street, adjacent to a companion site at 1980 Saturn Street (referred to in trade coverage as DigiCo 'LAX2') which is not listed as a separate record as of August 2026 - LAX2's specifics trace only to aggregator listings with no independent primary or press confirmation found as of August 2026; it is being divested in the same HMC Capital transaction. Capacity is disputed and not recorded: sources disagree materially (49.5-50 MW per Fox Business and No Data Center MPK, citing the applicant's own Initial Study/MND; approximately 56 MW per aggregators, apparently derived from 14 backup diesel generators at 4 MW each; 66-72 MW per CoStar describing 'the original proposal') and the primary withdrawal letter discloses no MW figure at all. Acreage is disputed and not recorded: approximately 5 acres per a community group's math from the building footprint versus 16 acres per Baxtel (aggregator-only - treated as unconfirmed). HMC Capital bought the parcel for approximately $39M (December 2024) and has agreed to sell it back for roughly $39M plus $33.5M for the adjacent LAX2 site plus a $10M contingent earn-out, settling in H1 FY27 - real-estate transaction values, not construction capex, since the facility was never built; no investment figure is recorded. No jobs figures have been disclosed. No AI/HPC-specific marketing language found for this project. City had a pre-existing data-center moratorium before this project surfaced. Coordinates are an approximate street-level geocode, not a parcel-confirmed point.

approval_context.text: Measure NDC, a permanent citywide data-center ban, passed 88.34% (10,321-1,362) in a June 2, 2026 special election and was implemented via Ordinance 2279; the applicant's withdrawal (March 31, 2026) preceded the vote. The community group 'No Data Center MPK' cited approximately 12 million gallons/year of water use, approximately 434 GWh/year of power draw, noise, and approximately 77,034 metric tons CO2e/year, sourced to the applicant's own Initial Study/MND.

notes: EdgeConneX's ~$1B multi-phase "MCN New Albany" South campus. Per the Ohio Tax Credit Authority scope-of-work filing: Phase I converts a ~525,000 sq ft existing warehouse (9850 Innovation Campus Way) into an 80 MW data center; Phase II proposes two new 72 MW facilities (144 MW) — the planned capacity is 224 (80 + 144, IT load). A co-located PowerConneX natural-gas energy center (reported 140–216 MW of generation across sources) is excluded from the capacity figure as on-site generation, not IT load. Footprint is the four EdgeConneX MCN New Albany South PropCo 2 LLC parcels (97.53 ac per the Licking County Auditor, incl. the 33.86 ac built anchor at 9850 Innovation Campus Way). As of October 2026, the adjacent North PropCo 1 parcel (3356 Clover Valley Rd NW, 170.29 ac) is tracked separately as the EdgeConneX New Albany North Campus. "MCN" is EdgeConneX's internal project prefix (not publicly decoded). Distinct from EdgeConneX's separate Piper Farms land (12 parcels, 136.38 acres in Monroe Township per the Licking County Auditor, deeded 2025-11-17; as of October 2026 about 2.8 mi from this campus's recorded point, and no cited source states its intended use) and from EdgeConneX's Ashville Campus (Pickaway County). Public reception, as of 2026-09-10: this is EdgeConneX's New Albany/Licking County campus (Innovation Campus Way; PowerConneX I (120 MW) and II (216 MW) serve this campus; PowerConneX New Albany 3 (OPSB lists 450 MW; an operator notice said up to 430 MW) serves the North Campus). It is a separate EdgeConneX project from the heavily-opposed EdgeConneX proposal in Ashville, Pickaway County, OH (denied annexation 2026-02-02 after packed council meetings and a Change.org petition). For New Albany/Licking County specifically, a 2025 article on EdgeConneX's separate Piper Farms land purchase (checked 2026-09-10) mentions only general Central Ohio-wide concern that data centers could raise electricity costs, immediately caveated because this project's power comes from dedicated on-site generation (PowerConneX), not the residential grid. No hearing, resident testimony, or official statement specific to this Licking County site was found.

status_history.note: Phase I warehouse conversion (80 MW) underway; Phase II (two new 72 MW buildings) proposed. Ohio TCA sales-tax exemption approved Oct 2025.

Mayor Carletta Davis committed to "transparency and open communication with residents." A public meeting was set for 11 June 2026 at Prichard City Hall. records.name: Empire AI Beta
records.operator: Empire AI consortium (hosted by the University at Buffalo, SUNY)
records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
notes: New York State-funded public AI supercomputer, the second phase (Beta) of the Empire AI consortium. UB states it is "housed at the Center of Excellence in Bioinformatics and Life Sciences on the medical campus"; coordinates are geocoded to that building on the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus, hence approximate. Described as "a $40 million NVIDIA-powered supercomputer" delivering "an 11-fold increase in AI training capacity, a 40-fold boost in AI inference and an 8-fold expansion in data storage" versus Alpha. As of 2026-09-09, none of the three retrieved sources states a GPU count, an IT load or any MW figure, a water/cooling detail, an acreage, or a job count for Beta. Empire AI overall is backed by "over $500 million in public and private funding"; that is consortium-wide, not this site, so it is not recorded as an investment figure. The Alpha phase (launched 2024, Simons Foundation gift) is also housed at UB and is the predecessor system on the same campus, not a separate site. The permanent Gamma facility is tracked separately as Empire AI Gamma as of September 2026. The governor's office states that the consortium's funding includes "up to $340 million in state capital funding"; that is a consortium-wide ceiling covering Empire AI statewide, not attributable to this phase or site, so it is not recorded and not counted against both the Beta and Gamma records. The $40 million Beta award, approved by the Empire State Development board, is recorded as the investment figure. It is a state grant to a public research consortium rather than an incentive to a company, so no subsidy entry is recorded.

status_history.note: Governor Hochul announced Empire AI Beta fully online.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. Crusoe Energy filed TCEQ air construction permit (TCEQ announcement Feb 5, 2026) for a 933 MW natural gas power plant on-site at the Goodnight campus. Gas plant operates off-grid with no ERCOT grid connection for this generation asset. No carbon capture technology. Estimated emissions up to 4.5 million tons CO2/year and 1,600 tons criteria air pollutants/year per permit application. A portion of the campus also co-locates behind the meter with Goodnight Wind farm (265.5 MW, Serena Energy, came online 2024) under Texas SB6 net metering arrangement; proposal submitted to Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), regulatory review ongoing as of mid-2026. Separate TCEQ wastewater permit WQ0016881001 filed under same entity, indicating water/utility infrastructure planning underway.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Campus name: Goodnight, near the town of Claude, TX (known address: 10001 Lima Rd, Claude, TX 79019). Coordinates approximate (county parcel area). Developed by Crusoe Energy via entity GN DC1, LLC (Delaware LLC, 255 Filmore St., Denver, CO 80206); Google is the hyperscale tenant/customer, confirmed publicly November 2025. Tax abatement agreement was signed with GN DC1, LLC in late 2024 without publicly naming the tenant. Google confirmed the Crusoe partnership but had not signed an offtake agreement for the on-site gas plant as of early 2026; negotiations on power amounts still ongoing per Google spokesperson. Planned IT capacity: Phase 1 described in tax abatement agreement as 'anticipated to consume up to 530 MW,' 4 buildings each with 4 x 25 MW data halls, on approximately 350 acres; Phase 2 (possible additional 3+ buildings) reported at up to ~500 MW additional; combined full build-out reported as 1 GW+ — all capacity figures are 'up to' ceilings from permit and abatement documents, not firm contracted amounts. Project was scaled back from an original 7-building plan (October 2025 local reporting); 4 buildings with construction permits from TDLR as of early 2026; Crusoe described 3-4 buildings as likely; grading on additional parcels suggests total program may reach 5+ buildings. First phase expected online 2026; initial county PILOT payment expected June/July 2026. The $40B Google Texas investment is a statewide commitment through 2027 covering multiple sites (Armstrong County, Haskell County, Ellis County) with no site-specific investment figure disclosed by Google. A $29B campus investment figure appeared in Aterio/Crusoe reporting — this is a projected ceiling, not a firm committed amount, so it is not recorded as an investment figure. Distinct from Google's separate Haskell County TX site and Red Oak (Ellis County) TX sites — do not conflate. Building 3 is scheduled for completion 2026-08-01; Building 4 is due March 2027. Nothing at the campus is yet described as operational.

approval_context.text: Armstrong County Commissioners Court approved the original tax abatement agreement unanimously at the November 12, 2024 public hearing. The amended PILOT structure was also approved unanimously in 2025 after hearing from elected officials from multiple taxing entities and members of the public. County Judge Adam Ensey publicly supported the amendment, noting it allows revenue collection to begin with each completed building rather than waiting for phase completion. Initial county payment expected June/July 2026.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: No water volume or cooling system type disclosed in sources reviewed. TCEQ wastewater permit WQ0016881001 filed under the same GN DC1 LLC entity, indicating water infrastructure is being permitted; no public details available on cooling approach or projected water consumption.

status_history.note: Armstrong County Commissioners Court approved tax abatement agreement with GN DC1, LLC (Crusoe Energy entity) at November 12, 2024 public hearing. Tenant not publicly named at that time.

Google confirmed partnership with Crusoe for Goodnight campus as part of $40B statewide Texas announcement, November 2025. Satellite imagery (Cleanview, Feb 24 2026) confirmed two buildings under active construction with roof installation and steel framing underway.

Location: the 2023 Baxtel report on Google's planning applications (filed under the alias Shalerock LLC) places the work between NE Parvin Road and N Arlington Avenue, and the land comprises 78.9 acres bought in 2019 plus 236.4 acres bought in December 2021 (315.3 acres in total). A third-party Baxtel listing gives 9900 NE Parvin Rd, which Nominatim and the Census geocoder could not resolve to a building, so it is not used; a 2019 Baxtel report separately describes the 78-acre parcel as the former AK Steel site near MO-210 and N Arlington Avenue. Code name 'Project Shale': appears in two 2019 reports (Institutional Real Estate, Inc. and Baxtel, both relaying local coverage of the 22 July 2019 Port KC board meeting) for the 78-acre Hunt Midwest parcel. The 2023 Baxtel report ties the same 78.9-acre 2019 purchase to Shalerock LLC, and Shalerock/Shale is consistent, but, as of October 2026, no 2024-2026 source consulted uses 'Project Shale' for the $1 billion campus, so the identification is an inference from the shared site, not a stated one (hence the record is marked reported). A local TV station (KLKN) confirms the site is 'currently operational with ongoing construction phases' with roughly 200 on-site personnel, and that Google has committed to work with the city on water infrastructure; the city says it is not currently approving additional data centers beyond this one. Caveat: widely repeated secondary figures for this project (codename 'Agate', ~580 acres, ~$600M, sited northwest of N. 56th St & I-80) come from outlets that were blocked or paywalled on direct retrieval as of August 2026 (Lincoln Journal Star/tollbit, Nebraska Examiner). Those numbers were not independently verified then and are omitted from the structured fields (capacity, investment, acreage) rather than risk propagating an unverified figure. Coordinates mark the N. 56th Street / I-80 interchange, where 1011 NOW places the cooling system and KLKN (2019) places the land northwest of the 56th Street exit; the building footprint itself is not pinned. Community reception, as of 2026-09-10: Google's own data center locations page describes community partnerships/workforce programs in generic marketing terms but documents no specific public hearing, resident testimony, or independently reported local reaction.
records.water_notes: Google is funding a $10 million, roughly three-mile dedicated line carrying non-contact cooling water from the data center's cooling system at 56th Street and Interstate 80 to Lincoln's Northeast Water Resource Recovery Facility at North 70th and McCormick Drive. The line is sized for 2,040 gallons per minute at peak — about 2.9 million gallons per day — and the water is dechlorinated and discharged to Salt Creek, bypassing standard wastewater treatment. Construction began June 2026 with completion expected January 2027. This is the discharge line's peak design capacity, NOT measured or reported facility water use; do not publish it as consumption. No cooling type is recorded: 'non-contact cooling water' does not map cleanly onto the evaporative/closed-loop/air distinction. Separately, 1011 NOW (published 2026-09-30) reports, from a filing by Agate LLC to the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy, and Environment (DWEE), that the site used 13.299 megagallons (about 13 million gallons) of water 'between cooling towers, evaporative systems and site operations in the last year'. The article does not name a calendar year for this figure, and the filing was reported on after its redacted text was recovered by copying; the figure is the operator's self-report, not an independent measurement. No daily water-use figure is recorded because no daily rate is stated.

records.name: Google Pryor Data Center Campus (Mayes County Expansion)
records.segment_basis: Hyperscale / cloud operator classification from the reported operator. Building scale and workload are not inferred.
notes: Campus operational since 2011; Google's second-largest data center globally per Alphabet CIO Ruth Porat. Four expansions now underway. $5.7B+ invested historically in Oklahoma prior to August 2025 $9B commitment. Expansion capacity and MW not publicly specified. Coordinates are Pryor city center.

approval_context.text: Strong official support — Pryor Mayor Zac Doyle: Google has brought "hundreds of jobs, economic growth, and billions in investment" and supports local schools and nonprofits. Google reports more than 800 jobs created to date in Pryor and $4.4 billion invested in Mayes County to date (company-provided figures via The Frontier). Grassroots and state-level concerns are documented: local hiring practices, rising housing costs, and heavy water use (>1.1B gal/yr); the Oklahoma Water Resources Board warned (Oct 2025) that data centers "will contribute to the strain" on water supply. Subsidy scale also criticized: ~$239M ad valorem for this facility, plus $113.9M in income-tax credits Google has claimed statewide since 2017.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Utility records (open-records request) show the Pryor center used more than 1.1 billion gallons Jul 2024–Jun 2025 (≈3.0 MGD, a floor) from the Neosho River via the state-owned MidAmerica Industrial Park; ~253M gallons were discharged back to the river, the remainder lost to evaporative cooling. Google was the park's second-largest water user that year.

status_history.note: Campus opens in Mayes County after first announcement in 2007. Has undergone three expansions since opening.
New expansion announced as part of Google's $9B, two-year Oklahoma investment commitment.
