notes: 1,700 acres both sides of Route 62, north end of Buffalo near the Kanawha River (address disclosed as 22272 Charleston Road). Announced March 2026 as a multibillion-dollar investment with no figure stated; State Treasurer Larry Pack's September 2026 report on data center tax revenue uses an estimated $7 billion total investment for the Google project, saying the project 'lacks investment specifics at the present time', so no investment figure is recorded; still in early due diligence. As of 2026-09-10, the status was unchanged (proposed). The most recent coverage found (an update dated 2026-09-03) still describes the site as an application under review, not a permitted or under-construction project. Capacity and water/cooling type remain unconfirmed: Google's own spokesperson has not disclosed power or water figures for this site as of the 2026-09-03 update. As of October 2026, neither West Virginia Public Broadcasting's reports nor Google's project site gives a site power-demand or water-volume figure: West Virginia Public Broadcasting reports plans for generating 100% of the electricity needed and treating 120% of the water needed, and that MN8 Energy said it will provide 86 megawatts of renewable energy to Google's data centers in the region; Google's project site gives its 100% and 120% figures only as company-wide commitments (it pays for 100% of the electricity its data centers use and aims to replenish 120% more freshwater than it consumes, on average, across its data centers and offices by 2030). No job count is recorded: officials cite only non-numeric 'thousands of construction jobs and hundreds of permanent roles,' and, as of September 2026, no source found gives integer counts. No AI classification is assigned: sources describe this as a general Google data center / cloud campus, and none of the sources reviewed as of September 2026 specifically frames this site as AI-dedicated (vs. general cloud). No facility-specific incentive/abatement program was found in any source reviewed as of September 2026; HB 2014's tax-revenue split (majority to state, county keeps roughly 30%) is a distribution of taxes the facility generates, not a subsidy granted to the facility, so it is not recorded as a subsidy.

approval_context.text: Named residents cited cancer/health fears and anger over the March 27, 2026 announcement, while the Buffalo mayor and a state delegate voiced enthusiastic support; no formal hearing or vote has occurred yet.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Google's project site states "We evaluate the local water source for each data center, using a science-based framework to assess watershed health" and that "our cooling decisions consider the local environment — balancing affordable energy and responsibly-sourced water." West Virginia Public Broadcasting reports a plan for "treating 120% of the water needed." No cooling method or withdrawal volume has been published for the Buffalo site, so no cooling type or water-use figure is recorded.

status_history.note: 1,700 acres on both sides of Route 62, north end of Buffalo near the Kanawha River; approved as a High Impact Development Project but still in due diligence/early stage.

notes: Pine Hill Business Campus, Research Center Drive and Highway 17A, Ridgeville. Planned as part of Google's overall $9B SC commitment through 2027 (announced October 2025). MW capacity not disclosed by Google. The September 2024 state announcement does not break investment out by site; $2B is the combined Dorchester County (Ridgeville + St. George) figure. A $510M investment figure appears in a February 2024 Data Center Dynamics report, citing the Post and Courier, on the 231-acre Ridgeville site, which predates that announcement. Live 5 News (WCSC) reported in October 2024 that the $510 million project would build both Dorchester campuses, one in Ridgeville and one in St. George, so it is not settled that $510M is a Ridgeville-only figure, and no investment figure is recorded. As of October 2026, the second Dorchester campus, at Winding Woods Commerce Park, St. George, is listed separately as Google Winding Woods Campus. Coordinates are Ridgeville area centroid. Google's own South Carolina data-center page states a Dorchester County facility 'opens' in 2024, which is difficult to reconcile with this record being listed as under construction as of 2026-08-26. Ridgeville and St. George (Winding Woods, the other Dorchester County Google site in this dataset as of September 2026) are both in Dorchester County and the source does not name which one it refers to, so the statement is not attributed to one site over the other and no status change is asserted. It is also plausible this describes an early operational phase of a multi-phase campus while the overall project legitimately remains listed as under construction. Newer local sources describe both Dorchester County campuses as still being built: the Charleston Regional Development Alliance's October 2025 announcement of Google's $9 billion investment calls them 'projects that are now under active construction', and Dorchester County's data center fact sheet (archived copy captured 29 July 2026) says 'The data centers are being built in phases'. As of October 2026, no source found other than Baxtel, an aggregator, describes the Ridgeville campus as operational, so it remains listed as under construction. As of September 2026, no capacity or jobs data was found for this site in targeted checks of Santee Cooper (newsroom, generation-projects, board-meetings [JS-rendered, not retrievable], IRP and economic-development pages -- none name Google or this project), the SC Governor's newsroom, SC Commerce newsroom, scbiz.com, Post and Courier (not retrievable), Live5/WCSC and ABCNews4/WCIV (client-side search surfaced no results) and the SC PSC docket system (its search requires an interactive form, which could not be submitted).

City-commissioned feasibility study found the grid can deliver only 45 MW within 24 months against Logistix's 240 MW request; Logistix asked the city to pause the study, stating no decision had been made on the project.

Butler County Commissioners' data-center moratorium coverage (moratorium covers only unincorporated townships, not the City of Hamilton) confirms the Hamilton project has been on pause since January 2026, with no resumption, cancellation, or construction start confirmed since.

notes: Proposed data center inside a mixed-use redevelopment of the 76-acre former Kenwood convent / Doane Stuart School property in Albany. No capacity is recorded: "Guild Ventures... filed an application with the New York Independent System Operator to use 180MW for the project," but the developer told CBS6 the 180 MW is "a theoretical ceiling for the entire mixed-use development" at full buildout and not the data center's expected use. Recording 180 as the facility's capacity would therefore be wrong. CBS6 reported in July 2026 that the developer has said the data center could use up to 100 MW; that is a ceiling, not a planned total, and at an August 2026 community meeting the developers said they did not yet know how many megawatts the data center would need (WAMC), so it is not recorded either. WAMC (August 2026) also reports the developers project a 250,000-square-foot data center with 125 to 175 full-time jobs and an online date of December 2028; these are developer projections and no size or job figure is recorded. The Rockefeller Institute's tracker separately describes it as "a 180 MW data center as part of a mixed-use development" - that reading conflicts with the developer's own clarification, which is why the record is marked reported. The developer describes the compute component as a "boutique, edge-scale colocation center" on "approximately 5 acres" of the 76-acre parcel serving hospitals, institutions, nanotech, government services and local employers - hence the mixed-use AI classification. The 76-acre figure is the whole redevelopment parcel, not the data center footprint. As of 2026-09-09, no permits had been submitted to the City of Albany per the reporting retrieved, and the May 2026 CBS6 article gives no investment figure and states no job counts, utility, or IDA/PILOT agreement. The connecting utility, National Grid, is stated in NYISO load queue #1754. Coordinates geocoded to the named Kenwood / Doane Stuart site in Albany, approximate.

capacityMw.planned: As of October 2026, the cited figures are ceilings, not a planned total: the developer calls the 180 MW NYISO request a theoretical ceiling for the whole mixed-use site, CBS6 (July 2026) reports it said the data center could use up to 100 MW, and WAMC (August 2026) reports the developers said they did not yet know how many megawatts it would need.

notes: Vermaland LLC is a Phoenix-area land developer and land-banking company (CEO Kuldip 'Ken' Verma, founded 2006, controls ~25,000 acres of metro Phoenix land). DCD explicitly noted 'it is unclear whether Vermaland would operate its own data center facilities' — Vermaland plans to sell or rent parcels/buildings to tenants. No end tenants or hyperscaler operators have been named as of July 2026. Original plan: 59 data centers, up to 3 GW capacity ceiling, up to $33B investment ceiling, 3,300-acre site south of Eloy along the Greene Canal. A separate adjacent 1,700-acre parcel already holds Industrial-2 zoning for data centers, gas plants, battery storage, and solar. After strong public opposition (all ~60 public comments opposed), operator announced May 2026 scale-back to 11 data centers and 1 GW ceiling. Board of Supervisors hearing scheduled August 26, 2026; no permits issued as of record date. Site lies adjacent to a Qualified Opportunity Zone (investor tax benefit; not a direct subsidy to Vermaland — no subsidy award confirmed, omitted). Coordinates are approximate (parcel south of Eloy city center along Greene Canal; no precise APN published). $33B investment and all GW figures are announced ceilings, not firm commitments.

approval_context.text: All approximately 60 public comments and 50 emails received by the Pinal County Board opposed the project. Concerns raised: location in a high-risk flood zone, wildlife and environmental impacts, water use risk, power bill impacts for local residents, construction timeline (gas plant likely last, 5-7 year timeline). Scale-back from 3 GW to 1 GW was a direct response to this opposition. Pinal County Supervisor Rich Vitiello expressed concern about constituent energy cost impacts.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.utility: Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) — proposed grid transmission line upgrades for interconnect. APS and SRP not confirmed as utility providers.
records.water_notes: Developer's attorney stated commitment to air-cooled or closed-loop cooling to minimize water demand. Site borders the Greene Canal, raising concerns about water access and consumption in an arid region. No MGD figures have been published. Critics cited Pima County's 'Project Blue' hyperscale data center as a cautionary precedent for water misuse in Arizona desert developments.

status_history.note: Vermaland publicly announces La Osa Project (DCD: Aug 4, 2025; AZ Big Media: Sep 15, 2025); rezoning application filed with Pinal County ~April 2025. $33B/3 GW ceiling figures publicized. Pinal County Planning & Zoning Commission holds non-voting informational session July 17, 2025.

April 17, 2026: Pinal County land-use committee recommends advancing to full rezoning and site-plan review. No construction authorization granted; comprehensive plan amendment, drainage, flood mitigation, and road improvements still required.

May 2026: Operator announces 80% scale-back after all ~60 public comments opposed the project — revised plan reduces to 11 data centers and a 1 GW energy demand ceiling (down from 59 DCs / 3 GW). Board of Supervisors hearing rescheduled to August 26, 2026.

The Pinal County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on August 26, 2026 to reject the La Osa Energy Center rezoning request and development plans, after the developer had already scaled the proposal back roughly 80% (from 59 data center buildings and 3 GW of demand to 11 buildings, a 500 MW gas plant, battery storage and a 1 GW cap) in response to opposition over aquifer drawdown and incomplete energy sourcing plans. Supervisor Stephen Miller cast the lone dissent. Recorded as cancelled because the entitlement the project required was denied; Vermaland has not publicly announced a withdrawal or a refiling, so this reflects the county's denial rather than a developer decision.

records.name: MACROHARDRR (xAI Southaven)
records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
notes: The City of Southaven's Mayor's Report of 2026-01-07 says this building "will become the home of their 3rd data center in the metropolitan area and the 2nd facility in Mississippi along with the renovated power plant at 2875 Stanton Road." It is distinct from xAI's power plant at 2875 Stanton Road (per the DeSoto Times and the Mayor's Report). MACROHARDRR retrofits an 810,000 sq ft former warehouse at 2400 Stateline Road. The Mayor's Report identifies it as the building formerly used by GXO; the DeSoto Times and Mississippi Free Press give the same 810,000 sq ft figure. The pin is the centroid of the OpenStreetMap building named "xAI Macrohardrr" on Stateline Road West, whose mapped outline measures roughly 810,000 sq ft (derived from the mapped OSM outline), matching the reported size; OpenStreetMap tags it with a Memphis, Tennessee address, which conflicts with the Mississippi address in every source. The DeSoto Times reports that Elon Musk broke the news of the building purchase on X on Dec. 30 (2025). Gov. Tate Reeves' office announced on 2026-01-08 a corporate investment "exceeding $20 billion" that "will create hundreds of permanent jobs throughout DeSoto County". The Governor's release announcing this data center says the Mississippi Development Authority "has approved xAI for its Data Center Incentive" (a sales and use tax exemption "for all computing and equipment software used by companies certified as data centers by the agency") and that the City of Southaven and DeSoto County "are also supporting xAI's projects through fee-in-lieu agreements". The Mississippi Free Press reports the data center "will initially employ 145 people"; the Governor's release says "hundreds of permanent jobs throughout DeSoto County". The release ties the exceeding-$20-billion investment to the Southaven project without breaking it down, so no investment figure is recorded for this building. The DeSoto Times reports that xAI purchased two pieces of property (47 and 58 acres) near its power plant at 2875 Stanton Road; that acreage is not clearly attributable to this building's own site, so the land area is omitted here rather than guessed. The Governor's release says that upon completion "the Southaven data center will increase the company's computing power to nearly 2 gigawatts", which is a company-wide total, and Musk's post (DeSoto Times) refers to xAI's training compute ("Will take @xAI training compute to almost 2GW."). Neither gives this building's own capacity, so no capacity is recorded. The Governor's release says the company "expects to begin data center operations in Southaven in February 2026." The January 2026 release also says xAI "has purchased and is retrofitting a building to house the new data center operations", so the record is under construction. No primary source reports the building operating, so operational is not claimed. The Baxtel aggregator page shows both Under Construction and Operational status badges and the text "Fully operational with expansion in progress"; this record follows the Governor's primary-source statement instead. Earlier versions of this site listed this building twice; as of October 2026, those entries are combined here.
records.water_notes: The City of Southaven's Mayor's Report, in its discussion of the Southaven development, addresses water supply but not the heat-rejection method: it says xAI will use water as a paying customer with strict capacity management, and that its needs will ultimately be met by its own solutions and cost with recycling options. As of October 2026, none of the sources consulted identifies evaporative, closed-loop or dry cooling, so the cooling type stays unknown.

status_history.note: The DeSoto Times reported that Musk broke the news on X on Dec. 30 that the company had acquired an 810,000 square foot warehouse at 2400 Stateline Road: "xAI has bought a third building called MACROHARDRR".
The Governor's office said xAI "has purchased and is retrofitting a building to house the new data center operations."

notes: Formerly referred to as Project Blackjack; sited on the Manse Road corridor near the southern entrance to Pahrump along Highway 160, roughly 1,100 feet from the nearest homes. Developer states $18.4 billion of capital investment at full buildout and $114 million in annual Nye County property taxes; a separate figure of $8.4 billion appeared in other reporting and had not been resolved as of August 2026, so the developer's own $18.4B is recorded. Design features include screening berms, rooftop parapets for sound reduction and a target of roughly 55 dB at the property line. No megawatt capacity has been disclosed. Construction was anticipated to begin in 2027 with a five-year buildout. On August 18, 2026, after a June 2026 county-wide moratorium on new data center applications, the Nye County Commission voted 5-0 to adopt Bill No. 2026-11, which prohibits data center development in the Pahrump Valley (Hydrographic Basin 162); Nevada Current reported that the ban was a blow to the Manse Technology Campus and would effectively prevent the development of any data centers in and around the town of Pahrump. As of October 2026, among the cited sources, none reports the developer withdrawing the project, and the developer's site still describes it as a proposed development, so the status remains proposed.

approval_context.text: Residents packed a July 2026 Nye County town hall and a subsequent county forum to object; a public petition opposing the project is circulating. Nye County adopted a moratorium on data center applications in June 2026 and a ban in water basin 162 on August 18, 2026.

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.

power.scope: facility / project; source scope requires verification
power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. Per the applicant at the May 2016 IIC meeting, the facility would 'mostly pull power from the PJM grid from Middletown' over 138 kV lines from an adjacent substation. An on-site natural-gas cogeneration plant would supply redundancy and peak-period power within air-permit hour limits. DBT and Data Center Knowledge (2015) give the gas plant as 52.5 MW. At the 2016 IIC meeting the applicant described the data center as 40 MW, with 36 MW of white space at a design PUE of 1.4, for a 50 MW total requirement at full build.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Never built, and apparently dormant since the air-permit application was put on hold in October 2017. The record stays listed as proposed because, as of October 2026, no source records a formal withdrawal or cancellation. Treat the status as stalled, not active. The state grant was approved at up to $7.5M (the committee minutes record the request as "up to $7,500,000") and was conditional and reimbursement-only, so no grant amount is recorded. As of October 2026, no evidence was found that it was disbursed, so the record lists it as the IIC's May 2016 approval, not as money paid. Sources disagree on cost: $250M (DCK 2015), about $400M (DBT 2015) and $350M (applicant, IIC 2016). The recorded investment figure is the applicant's $350M estimate, which the AP also reported in May 2016. Jobs figures are the applicant's 2016 IIC projections. DBT 2015 cited 'more than 100' full-time and up to 2,000 construction jobs. Partners named at the IIC meeting were Duffield Associates (now Verdantas), MEP Associates and landowner Mautom, LLC. The end operator was never disclosed. The pin is Middletown's OSM boundary centroid, because the 70-acre Westown parcel did not resolve to a point.

approval_context.text: Residents opposed the gas plant over air emissions and property values. Two petitions gathered 530 signatures (2015), and members of the public questioned taxpayer funding for a company with undisclosed financiers (2016).
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: Middletown Town Council approved plans for the Middletown Technology Center: a 228,000 sq ft, 40 MW data center with a natural-gas cogeneration plant on 70 acres in the town's Westown area. Delaware Infrastructure Investment Committee voted 4-0 to approve up to $7.5M in New Jobs Infrastructure Fund money for the project's utility infrastructure. The approval was conditioned on a DNREC air permit, financing disclosure, identification of the operator, and payment on a reimbursement basis.
Per the dcmap.us activity log, Cirrus put its Middletown air-permit application on hold. No later activity was found.

notes: Possible overlap with an existing record. NCPR states "the facility would include three buildings totaling nearly 1.5 million square feet at the former Reynolds site, about eight miles outside of the village of Massena and near the bridge to Canada. The operation would consume 635 megawatts of power. That equates to roughly 70% of the power produced at the Moses-Saunders Power Dam. The developer, North Country Collocation Services, or NCCS, presented its plan to the board." The former Reynolds Metals plant is the same industrial complex as the 'Alcoa East' site that the existing Coinmint (Massena East / former Alcoa Smelter) crypto-mining record sits on (that record is at 44.9777, -74.7327), and NCPR (October 7, 2026) reports that NYDIG and its affiliate NCCS want to build the data center, captioning a photo of the former Alcoa East site as "now being acquired by NYDIG". It is recorded as a separate proposed data center because the three buildings, the 635 MW load and the planning-board proceeding are a distinct new project with a distinct developer entity. Coordinates are an approximate placement on that industrial complex derived from the source's description, not a surveyed parcel. As of 2026-09-09, the sources retrieved stated no investment figure, no job counts, no acreage, no water-use figure, no utility, and no subsidy or IDA agreement. A North Country Public Radio report of October 7, 2026 gives the company's figures of 200 full-time jobs and an estimated 2,000 construction jobs. Reporting elsewhere describes 316 diesel generators on site and a zoning question referred to the Zoning Board of Appeals over whether a large-scale data center is a permitted use in the industrial zone; neither is recorded because, as of September 2026, neither had been verified.

approval_context.text: NCPR reports "about 80 people" attended the May 21, 2026 planning board meeting, that "some shouted their opposition and questions from the audience," and quotes a resident of Akwesasne (the Mohawk territory less than two miles from the site) asking for more community engagement. The meeting was not a public hearing; the board chair said a public hearing will follow and "the process could take months." A residents' group, Massena Data Center Watch, campaigns against the project.

records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.
records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Rezoning request by Akin & Tate P.C. on behalf of Oakley Real Estate Partners for about 111.4 acres at the west end of Brown Farm Road, near the Etowah River, from A-1 (agricultural) to Business Park District, with a land-use-map change from low density residential to industrial. Oakley described it as a micro-scale data center it intends to market; no end user has been named. The plan is two buildings of about 374,000 sq ft in total, with a power substation and a single access drive, and a voluntary condition that the campus never exceed 450,000 sq ft. Other self-imposed conditions: setbacks of at least 200 ft from residential areas, and no cryptocurrency mining. Oakley estimated about 50 jobs and roughly $5 million a year in property taxes. At the Planning Commission hearing, Oakley said the substation and the nearest building would each sit 400 ft from the riverbank. The hearing was first set for 2026-07-27 but was removed from that agenda after county staff found a discrepancy in the notice sent to Native American nations with ties to the district. The Planning Commission voted 6-0 to recommend denial on 2026-08-24; the commissioner's 2026-09-02 agenda listed zoning applications, but as of 2026-09-30 neither the meeting minutes nor any press report of the final decision had been found. No Georgia DRI filing exists for the project. No capacity or investment figure has been disclosed. Coordinates are the western end of Brown Farm Road SW in OpenStreetMap, the location the press gives for the site, not a surveyed parcel centroid.

approval_context.text: The 2026-07-15 community meeting drew a standing-room crowd, and the residents who spoke were opposed, citing noise, water use, environmental effects, falling property values and the future of the area's historic district; opponent Alex Payne said the developers "paint a nice pretty picture" but leave questions about who will ultimately use the facility. At the 2026-08-24 Planning Commission hearing, moved to Courtroom D to accommodate a crowd that packed it to capacity, nearly everyone present was in opposition. Board member Richard Fox read that State Rep. Matthew Gambill (District 15) had submitted a letter opposing the project. Resident Marty Knight cited the Cherokee Darter, "a federally-listed threatened freshwater fish native exclusively to the Etowah River." Cartersville resident Howard Smith was the only community member to speak in favor. The commission voted 6-0 to recommend denial.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Developer-stated: closed-loop cooling that recirculates a fixed volume of water, with yearly water use estimated at around 10,000 gallons ("about the amount of water in a residential pool"), drained about once a year to the sanitary sewer. The developer said the site stays out of the FEMA regulatory floodway and the river keeps its vegetated stream buffers.

status_history.note: Akin & Tate P.C., on behalf of Oakley Real Estate Partners, applied to rezone about 111.4 acres off Brown Farm Road from A-1 to Business Park District and to change the land use map from low density residential to industrial; Oakley presented the plan at a 2026-07-15 community meeting. On 2026-08-24 the Bartow County Planning Commission voted 6-0 against both requests, sending recommendations for denial to the sole commissioner for a final decision at his 2026-09-02 meeting.

notes: Retrofit of a former Walmart Supercenter in Fairfield into a colocation data center. WBRC states: "Patmos would bring around 50 long-term jobs, plus roughly 120 construction workers during the build" and "If approved, construction could start in September, with the first phase completed by January or February 2027 and a larger expansion planned for 2028." WBRC gives no capacity or investment figure. WBHM (14 Aug 2026) reports that Patmos expects an initial 20 MW phase costing about $150 million and a site that eventually reaches 45 MW; the record carries the 45 MW full-buildout figure, and the $150 million investment figure covers only the initial 20 MW phase. WBRC attributes about 120 construction workers to the Fairfield build, while WBHM reports that figure as the peak construction workforce at Patmos's Kansas City project, so no construction-job figure is recorded. As of October 2026, the only street address, 7201 Aaron Aronov Dr, comes from the Baxtel listing; neither news account repeats it, and it geocodes to Western Hills Mall in OpenStreetMap, so it is not confirmed as the former Walmart and no street address is recorded. COORDINATES ARE THE FAIRFIELD MUNICIPAL CENTROID, not the building: the news sources identify the site only as "the former Walmart Supercenter" without a street address, and as of September 2026 no Walmart-named or former-retail building was found in OpenStreetMap within Fairfield's bounds. STATUS: the record is listed as proposed — construction was conditional on approval as of 13 Aug 2026, and as of September 2026 it was not confirmed whether the September 2026 groundbreaking happened. This is a genuinely distinct site from QTS Bessemer (Project Marvel) — different operator, different city — though both sit in the same Birmingham-west corridor.

approval_context.text: WBRC (13 Aug 2026) reports "Hundreds pack Fairfield town hall over proposed data center inside former Walmart", with residents raising health risks, rising utility bills and community benefit. Patmos's founder answered noise concerns by saying "you'll hear the equivalent of a weed wacker" when generators run and that operations would be "quieter than the Walmart"; Patmos said "the only environmental impact is water use." Resident Bessie Bell questioned whether the project would help Fairfield's development. Mayor Herman Carnes said the city has "not seen major economic development in roughly 15 years" and promised transparency. NOTE the city council had already passed a temporary data center ban, from which this project was exempt — community reception is recorded as contested rather than opposed because the friction is documented and organized in public meetings but no vote against this project is reported.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Patmos officials said the initial 20 MW phase would use about 10,000 gallons of water per day (WBHM, August 2026). That is a company estimate for a facility not yet built, so no water-use figure is recorded. Most cooling water would circulate through closed-loop systems, with some lost to evaporation.

records.name: PORTS-Pike Technology Campus
records.segment_basis: Physical scale is classified only when a source reports MW; no capacity is inferred from operator name or floor area.

power.note: Disclosed source-record capacity; not measured demand. S-1: the campus is "designed to include 8.0 GW-IT of data center capacity, representing 10 GW of gross power load expected to be supported by the PJM transmission system and new neighboring gas-fired generation facilities" - hence the energy source is recorded as a mix of sources. The 9.2 GW of gas is new build, not a reused plant; the site is the former Portsmouth uranium-enrichment complex, whose historic power came over OVEC coal-fired transmission (X-533 switchyard, de-energised 2008, decommissioned 2011). Recorded under on-site generation as dedicated captive generation, but note the S-1 calls the plants "neighboring": they sit ~5 miles south of Piketon adjacent to the DOE site, are developed by "an affiliate of SoftBank that is not our subsidiary", and SB Energy "do[es] not expect to own or operate" them. Ohio Power Siting Board case 26-0746-EL-BGN (applicant Portsmouth Gas DevCo, LLC) covers only a first tranche of "up to 2 gigawatts"; as of October 2026 OPSB's case-tracking data lists 1,770 MW in 48 units on 775 acres for that case, its application took effect 2026-10-15, a local public hearing is set for 2026-12-10 in Piketon and the evidentiary hearing for 2027-01-06, and at least nine petitions for leave to intervene were filed on 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-14 (the docket entry titles do not state their positions); a second case by the same applicant, 26-1070-EL-BGN, was opened 2026-10-15 and lists 5,000 MW with no application date; AEP Ohio transmission is separate from the generation case: AEP's Piketon Area Improvements hub lists the Baku-Gavin 765 kV line (OPSB 26-0426-EL-BTX), a planned Hanging Rock-Baku 765 kV line (26-0870-EL-BTX), the Baku 765 kV and Monza 345 kV stations, and two Baku extension lines (26-0866/0867/0868/0869-EL-BLN); an earlier description cited "four substations". AEP grid capex is stated as $4.2B by DOE and ~$5.1B in the S-1, unreconciled. CAUTION: the project site states the gas generation "will be owned by the U.S. Government", but the S-1 says "no binding agreement has been executed between us or any of our affiliates and any governmental entity with respect to the funding, construction, ownership or operation of the generation facilities" - do not assert federal ownership. Only ~0.8 GW of gross load has contracted utility service so far.

notes: Officially "PORTS-Pike Technology Campus"; formerly tracked under the pre-announcement Ohio entity New Day Data Centers LLC, a name that appears nowhere in the SEC S-1 or SB Energy’s own announcements. Developer/operator is SB Energy (SoftBank-controlled); the DOE lease was signed 2026-02-26 by its subsidiary Pike County Portsmouth DC LLC. Capacity: three distinct figures: 8.0 GW-IT of contracted compute (8,024 MW-IT; NVIDIA guarantees the initial 4.25 GW-IT with an option on the remaining 3.78 GW-IT), 10 GW of gross power load (the planned capacity recorded here), and 9.2 GW of new gas generation. Offtake: on 2026-08-17 SB Energy subsidiaries signed 17 twenty-year triple-net leases with OpenAI, with rent commencement conditioned on interconnection and generation being available; NVIDIA provided a residual-value guaranty capped at $105B and separately bought $1.5B of non-voting stock. Land: the land area is not recorded - the DOE lease covers 189 acres (Batch 1) on which "one data center building is expected to be constructed", while the S-1 places the buildings "across several thousand acres of private property"; the widely-cited 3,700/3,777 acres is the whole federal reservation, which also hosts the separately tracked Oklo Aurora project, Centrus and the DUF6 plant. Investment: no investment figure is recorded - $10B (DOE, March) and $30-40B (project site) describe the same ~800 MW first phase and cannot both be right, the $67.2B total appears only as one trade outlet’s unattributed rollup, and the S-1 states no total capex. Subsidies: none awarded - the Ohio Tax Credit Authority minutes record no award, no JobsOhio award was found as of September 2026, and Ohio paused new data-centre tax exemptions in May 2026; a county PILOT is under negotiation because the leased federal land yields no property tax. Status: early civil works began after the 2026-03-20 groundbreaking, though the S-1 lists construction as not started, with first capacity in 2028 and full buildout 2032. Distinct from the Oklo Aurora Powerhouse on the same broader site.

approval_context.text: Documented local support alongside contamination-legacy distrust. Support: State Sen. Shane Wilkin - "It’s just going to be a generational change for this area"; SODI executive director Steve Shepherd called it "a model for the country"; the Scioto Valley-Piketon Area Council of Governments chair framed it as moving contaminated residential land to industrial use. Concern: a neighbouring farmer with contaminated property ("This is the most contaminated place around here"), and Conserve Ohio on water, transmission and the precedent of siting hyperscale projects on legacy DOE land. TRANSMISSION: the lines serving the campus are being sited by the utility, AEP Ohio Transmission Company, not by the data center operator; the customer has committed to pay for them. Three corridors: Baku-Gavin 765 kV (Pike, Jackson, Gallia; OPSB Case 26-0426-EL-BTX, application filed 2026-07-24 and found complete 2026-08-28, local public hearing set for 2026-10-27 in Jackson, with an administrative law judge entry of 2026-10-21 granting an individual's petition to intervene and OPSB Staff's report of investigation filed 2026-10-22); Hanging Rock-Baku 765 kV (Pike, Scioto, Lawrence; AEP plans to file as 26-0870-EL-BTX); and an earlier-stage feasibility study in Pike, Ross and Pickaway counties with no route selected. As of 2026-10-15 no appropriation (eminent domain) filing against landowners for these lines was found (as of October 2026, county court dockets had not been checked); AEP describes acquiring right-of-way with just compensation, and Ohio law has treated AEP's Ohio Power Company as authorised to appropriate property for transmission easements (Ohio Power Co. v. Burns, 2022, an unrelated Washington County line). No litigation, moratorium or public-hearing defeat found as of 2026-10-15; a statewide watchdog notes this project lacks the named opposition groups seen elsewhere in Ohio. Community money (not a public subsidy to the operator): a $40M Community Benefits Agreement from SB Energy plus an incremental $40M from OpenAI.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

PH95-specific press materials do not name the utility. Rappahannock Electric Cooperative also serves parts of Spotsylvania County and cannot be ruled out.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Campus located at approximately 4189 Turner Ct, Spotsylvania County, VA along the I-95/Hwy 17 corridor; coordinates are approximate. Three 300 MW substations planned (800 MW total); first substation delivering 150 MW targeted for Q4 2025. Up to 8 buildings, 3.5 million sq ft. Phased delivery Q3 2025–Q4 2027. Joint venture between PowerHouse/AREP and Harrison Street. Harrison Street managing director explicitly cited 'high-powered computing, AI, and other advancements' as the demand driver for this campus class, supporting likely AI classification. Named tenant not disclosed. Dominion Energy utility attribution is inferred from service territory: Dominion's Tributary 230 kV project was approved by Virginia SCC (June 30, 2024) specifically to serve growing Spotsylvania data center demand; PH95 press materials do not name the utility directly. Investment amount, job figures, and water draw not disclosed in any sourced press materials. Joint venture: American Real Estate Partners (AREP) and Harrison Street.

approval_context.text: Spotsylvania County has experienced significant data center controversy: the board voted 4-3 in December 2025 to approve design standards; required special use permits for data centers in February 2026 (mirroring Loudoun, Prince William, and Henrico); public comments cited noise, grid strain, water supply risk, and visual impact. One project (Hunters Ridge South, 2.2M sq ft) passed 5-2 in August 2025. PowerHouse 95 itself was not identified as the specific target of organized opposition in sourced materials — it appears to have proceeded under earlier by-right industrial zoning rules. Rappahannock Electric Cooperative CEO told Spotsylvania officials that one data center can require as much energy as REC's entire customer base during peak demand.

records.water_notes: Press materials do not disclose cooling approach for PH 95 specifically. PowerHouse has deployed direct-to-chip and closed-loop cooling at other campuses; no water draw figures available.

notes: Speculative; the record is marked rumored. A proposed AI/semiconductor industrial campus with its own private power plant, before the Mississippi PSC. Prado told Mississippi Today he declined to give the PSC more detail because 'making that information available to the utility companies would take away the project's competitive advantage,' and Prado AI 'is still working on securing all the funding it would need for a project of this size'; the only figure attached to it is Prado's stated long-term goal of 'over $25 billion', which is an aspiration, not an announced investment, and is therefore not recorded as an investment figure. The project is docketed at the PSC and formally opposed by both of the state's major utilities, which is more than a press rumour. A separate facility, Traceview Advanced Power Station, is also in Ridgeland and is unrelated.

approval_context.text: Not a residents-vs-site dispute: the documented opposition is regulatory and commercial. Entergy Mississippi and Mississippi Power, the state's two largest power providers, are protesting the effort, arguing the arrangement would make Prado AI a public utility subject to PSC regulation, and that a certificate of public convenience and necessity would be required to build the generator. Mississippi Power's brief warned the request 'could intentionally or unintentionally upset this delicate regulatory balance.' No public-reception evidence from nearby residents appears in the source.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: Prado AI, an affiliate of PraCon Global Investment, asked the Mississippi Public Service Commission for an opinion on whether it would be regulated as a public utility if it generated and supplied power to tenants at a potential data center and semiconductor manufacturing campus; its initial filing said the campus would be in Ridgeland and that electricity would be included in the lease and not metered.

The PSC declined to issue an opinion, calling the request 'premature' and 'hypothetical' and saying it lacked enough information; Commissioner De'Keither Stamps said Prado did not answer basic questions such as how many tenants the power would serve. Prado said the company will proceed anyway.

notes: Unincorporated Pima County, west of Houghton Rd, near Tucson. Construction Review Online lists "Up to 286–600 MW (initial phases lower)" across "approximately 2 million square feet at full build-out", and the Pima County Administrator's memo of September 17, 2025 describes Tucson Electric Power's proposed Energy Supply Agreement as "supplying 286 megawatts (MW) of electricity from existing TEP capacity for the initial phase"; no single planned total is recorded. AWS confirmed as end-customer via an NDA obtained by AZ Luminaria. Distinct site from Beale Infrastructure's Fremont Peak Properties/Luckett Road project in the Town of Marana (also AZ, and also tracked as of August 2026) - same developer family, different parcel. Coordinates are approximate. The 180 permanent jobs figure is a projection for the third year of operations in 2029, published by Pima County and by the developer. Beale's own letter of 2025-09-17 adds a qualifier the county FAQ omits: the figure "include[s] full-time contractors and support personnel", and at least 75 of the roles will be directly employed by the end user. Beale has also stated it "is not asking for property tax incentives, often a necessary component of a data center project's cost competitiveness", and the utility agreement with Tucson Electric Power carries no financial incentives or discounts, which is unusual for a project of this size. Subsidies are therefore recorded as absent rather than merely unsearched.

capacityMw.planned: The cited sources give a range or an initial-phase figure, not a single planned total: Construction Review Online lists "Up to 286–600 MW (initial phases lower)", and the Tucson Electric Power agreement covers 286 MW for the initial phase.

notes: Proposed hyperscale data center campus on the former Tailgate Ranch in unincorporated Leavenworth County, south of Tonganoxie and south of the Tonganoxie Business Park, near the Tonganoxie/Eudora interchange on I-70. Reported as roughly 1,000 acres (KSHB; the Lawrence Journal-World writes "more than 1,000 acres" and the community lead that flagged the site claimed 1,100 acres; as of September 2026, no source found states 1,100, so 1,000 is recorded and the discrepancy is noted here). KSHB reports 330 acres set aside for permanent land conservation. The planned capacity recorded here is the reported ceiling: a revised proposal submitted after Leavenworth County's data center moratorium expired in August 2026 roughly doubled the project's electricity demand to "up to 1.2 gigawatts" and added an on-site gas power plant; a lower figure appears in one Journal-World reference ("600-watt data center", evidently a units error in the source) and is not used. Location precision is approximate: as of September 2026, no source found states coordinates, a street address or a parcel, so the pin is the Tonganoxie town centroid (OpenStreetMap/Nominatim) and the actual footprint lies some distance south of it. Cloverleaf Infrastructure, a Houston-based developer founded by former Microsoft energy executives, describes itself as a site-preparation developer that will introduce an end user later; no hyperscale tenant has been named. Cloverleaf's own site describes a "multi-billion-dollar taxable investment" but states no dollar figure, so no investment figure is recorded. As of 2026-09-23 the project is conceptual: Cloverleaf's FAQ states no formal applications have been submitted to local jurisdictions, and the county's data center planning and zoning regulations are not finalized.

approval_context.text: Organized local opposition. More than 1,000 people attended a Leavenworth County special meeting at the Tonganoxie Fairgrounds on 2026-09-16 for neighbor input; roughly 65 residents spoke and comments were predominantly against the project. Two opposition groups are named in reporting: the Tongie Data Center Watch Dog Group and Citizens Against Bluestem. Residents previously petitioned for an 18-month moratorium on data centers, and a temporary moratorium expired in August 2026. Stated concerns include noise, energy use, water use, property values, waste heat, and the site's proximity — reported as 1 to 1.5 miles — to Tonganoxie's elementary and middle schools and a nursing home.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Applicant of record is Taurus DC SPE LLC (Bartow County rezoning case Z-25-00020); no source reviewed names a parent company for that entity. Operator: Bartow County's August 2026 policy statement refers to the campus as "Digital Realty's investment in the Stilesboro area". The county's minutes of the June 4, 2025 hearing, summarizing the presentation by the applicant's attorney, Scott Peters, record: "This is a Digital Realty project. It is not a Crypto center.", and Andrew Alves of Digital Realty appeared as part of the Project Bunkhouse team at the May 19, 2025 planning commission hearing (Daily Tribune). Digital Realty has not announced the project in its own press releases. Property owner per the DRI filing: Gaines Family Land LLC; the DRI's developer field names Brian B. West of Kimley-Horn (engineering consultant). Site: Taff Road south of GA Hwy 113, south of Georgia Power's Plant Bowen, also bordering Floyd Creek Church Road; tax parcels 0032-1184-001, 0032-1122-001, 0032a-003-002 and 0032b-003-006; Raccoon Creek runs along the property. Coordinates are the point stated in the DRI filing, not a surveyed site centroid. Size: the DRI filing states 8,675,000 sq ft; the approved rezoning caps total building area at 8,300,000 sq ft. Capacity: Bartow County's August 2026 data-center policy statement says "Digital Realty's investment in the Stilesboro area, planned for approximately 1.3 gigawatts of computing capacity, has indicated a total build-out capital investment on the order of eighteen billion dollars," and that Digital Realty "forecasts total employment in excess of 800 jobs once the campus is complete"; the 1.3 GW is recorded as planned capacity. Earlier, a site plan obtained by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution (April 2025) put the project's power needs at 1,830 MW with three on-site substations; the DRI filing's energy-demand field is blank. The same county statement says Bartow County has granted no tax abatements, PILOT or comparable arrangement to these data center facilities. Value: the DRI filing states an estimated build-out value of $19 billion and projected annual property tax of at least $40-50 million, with build-out estimated for 2035. Incentives: the DRI filing said the project was "in the process of incentive negotiations" with the Bartow-Cartersville Joint Development Authority; the county's economic development director, Melinda Lemmon, said that was "mistakenly included in the DRI filing" and that the authority "is not negotiating incentives with the data center calling themselves Project Bunkhouse or any other data center" (Daily Tribune, April 2, 2025). No bond validation, PILOT or abatement for the project has been found. Rezoning conditions include: an 8,300,000 sq ft cap; buffers required before occupancy; primary access from Taff Road only; distribution, manufacturing, warehousing, outdoor storage, towers, laboratories and retail prohibited; water-efficient HVAC required. Other DRI figures: about 8,588 average daily vehicle trips, about 29% impervious surface, wetlands, floodplain and historic resources present on site (impacts not expected per the filing). No building permits or site work have been reported since the rezoning.

approval_context.text: Residents opposed the project at both public hearings. At the May 19, 2025 planning commission hearing, Valerie Holt, Amy Tilley and Lauren Van Winkle spoke against it (rural character, Taff Road traffic), and Joe Harris spoke in support of the landowners' right to sell; the commission still recommended approval unanimously (Daily Tribune). At the June 4, 2025 hearing, Patty Everett spoke in opposition, citing the loss of pasture and property values, and Gail Cochran asked whether Georgia Power would take her property for new transmission lines; the minutes record no other speakers. The sole commissioner approved the rezoning the same day. No petition, lawsuit or appeal specific to this project has been found.

notes: Subsidy: no formal abatement request had been filed as of 24 July 2026, according to Yellowhammer News, which reports that the granting body would be the Lowndes County Commission. Under legislation signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April 2026, an abatement approved before 1 January 2027 could run up to 30 years; after that date the maximum is 20 years. In October 2026 the Lowndes County Commission voted 3-2 to approve the tax abatements and project agreement; AL.com, republished by GovTech, reports the county granted "more than $1.1 billion in tax abatements", including 50% of the county non-educational property tax and the construction and server equipment refresh sales and use tax. No named tenant: Yellowhammer describes Cloverleaf as a Houston- and Seattle-based speculative developer assembling land for an unnamed future operator; the AI classification is therefore likely, not confirmed. Investment is "$1.5 billion" per WSFA and Route Fifty ("at least $1.5 billion in the development stage"), which is the floor recorded. The developer's own site, which said "Over a $1 billion taxable investment in Lowndes County" in September 2026, states no investment figure as of October 2026. Jobs: as of October 2026 the developer's site says the project will employ "more than 1,000 construction workers" and that full-time roles "will grow from 225 initially to over 300 at full scale"; the recorded figures are those floors (more than 1,000 construction jobs, over 300 full-time jobs at full scale). Other coverage that could not be retrieved as of September 2026 cites 1,000-1,500 construction and over 200 permanent jobs. Footprint: "more than 800 acres in northeast Lowndes County" and "2.88 million square feet" (Yellowhammer). Zoning: reporting notes Cloverleaf could buy and develop here because Lowndes County has no planning or zoning authority. Coordinates are the OSM-confirmed U.S. 80 / AL 21 junction that WSFA names as the site vicinity, not a parcel boundary; the actual footprint is somewhere in northeast Lowndes County near that junction.
capacityMw.planned: The 1,500 MW figure is a power request to the utility, not a stated IT capacity, so no planned capacity is recorded.

approval_context.text: Route Fifty (25 Aug 2026): "About 350 people signed the group's petition demanding more transparency from the commission" — the group is Protect Lowndes County, which filed an open-records request on 27 July 2026 seeking project documentation and entity lists. A separate campaign site (45strong.net) titled "Cloverleaf, withdraw from Lowndes County" appeared in search results but was not reviewed and is not cited. Yellowhammer News notes the site is "half a mile from a field where Selma-to-Montgomery marchers camped in 1965" and that the access road is the Robert "Bob" Mants Jr. Memorial Highway.

notes: The data-center tenant is not confirmed. We don't know what it's going to power yet... It potentially could be a data center, but it very well could be something else," naming advanced manufacturing, robotics and semiconductor manufacturing as alternatives, before adding that with that much power "it's very likely going to be that." The company's own 2026-08-26 release describes the campus as "anchored by an on-site power plant and data center." The record is marked reported for that reason. Roughly 850 acres of privately-owned Wright family land west of I-75 and north of Old Lower River Road NW, along the Hiwassee River in northern Bradley County near I-75 Exit 33, submitted for rezoning and annexation into the City of Cleveland on 2026-08-25. notes: Six buildings totaling 2,274,000 sq ft (about 379,000 sq ft each), per DRI #4403, which states the project "will utilize closed loop technology to reduce water and sewer demand." The DRI states a build-out value of $4,500,000,000 and completion in December 2031, and leaves the electrical-load and energy-provider fields blank. The 432 MW figure (six buildings of up to 78 MW each) is from press reporting on the site plan, not the DRI. Property owners per the DRI: The Darryl William Edwards Living Revocable Trust, King Curtis LLC and Riverside NVR LLC. Acreage: the county's minutes and the Daily Tribune give 630 acres for the rezoning request (to Business Park District); earlier press gave 588. Coordinates are the point stated in the DRI filing, not a surveyed site centroid. No named end-user operator was attached to the project. Distinct from Atlas Development's later Stiles Road application off Euharlee Road (withdrawn December 2025).

approval_context.text: Residents organized against the rezoning. A change.org petition, "Halt Proposed Land Use Change from Agriculture to Industrial in Bartow County", co-founded by Josh Cauthen, had 1,280 signatures by 2025-03-11 and 1,723 by 2025-03-21, and was reported at over 2,000 by the 2025-04-28 hearing. "The local community is in lockstep against the proposed rezoning," Cauthen said. Residents cited wildlife, well water and the prospect of further industrial rezoning nearby; Atlas's attorney put turnout at its 2025-03-19 town hall at "maybe 20 to 25 people." At the 2025-04-28 planning commission hearing, residents packed the room, many wearing red, and Barnsley Resort president David Friederich called the project "an existential threat" to the resort's business model. The commission voted 6-1 to recommend denial, and Atlas withdrew before the commissioner's decision.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: DRI #4403 estimates 0.015 MGD (15,000 gallons per day) water demand from Bartow County and zero sewage flow, and describes closed-loop technology.

status_history.note: Bartow County submitted Development of Regional Impact #4403 ("Project Springbank", developer Atlas Development LLC) to the Georgia DCA; determined to warrant regional review 2025-02-24.

Atlas Development withdrew rezoning application Z-25-00006 through its attorney on 2025-05-13, the day before the sole commissioner was to rule, after the Bartow County Planning Commission voted 6-1 on 2025-04-28 to recommend denial. Atlas gave no reason. No refiling of this site has been found.

approval_context.text: DNREC Secretary denied Coastal Zone Act permit February 4, 2026 citing 516 backup diesel generators and 2.5 million gallons of stored diesel as unprecedented heavy industrial use under Delaware's 1971 Coastal Zone Act. notes: Codename: Project Marvel. 18-building hyperscale campus on Red Ridge near I-459 and I-20/59 interchange in Bessemer (Jefferson County). Announced capacity: up to 1,200 MW at full build-out — reported as a planned ceiling, roughly 9% of Alabama Power's current generating capacity; recorded as a planned capacity of 1,200 MW (an announced 'up to' full-build-out ceiling, consistent with how the dataset records other announced full-build-out figures). Investment: TPA Group's Adam Rashid told the Bessemer City Council in November 2025 that the overall capital investment is expected to be $14.5 billion (WBRC), and that figure is recorded as the investment figure; other reports put it at about $14–14.4B (Logistics Land Investment anticipated 'close to $14.4B'; DCD reported ~$14B), and QTS's own July 2026 statement gives no dollar amount. Land: ~1,607.42 acres total after two rezoning rounds (initial ~700 acres November 2025 + 914-acre expansion April 2026). QTS affiliate purchased land from TPA Group affiliate for $431.73M. Chapter 9B statutory eligibility would have provided a 30-year abatement estimated at $500M+; QTS committed not to seek local property tax incentives (per WBRC July 2026) — no subsidy is recorded, as eligibility does not equal award and QTS renounced pursuit. Full buildout timeline: 7+ years. Birmingham Business Alliance estimated ~$4B net benefit over 30 years; Bessemer City Schools projected ~$25M/year. AI framing not officially confirmed by QTS or the city as of July 2026 — size and scale (hyperscale, cloud/AI demand framing in QTS statement) support an AI classification of likely. Coordinates are approximate for the Red Ridge parcel area. Jobs: ~1,000 construction and ~330 permanent are projected figures for the proposed (not-yet-built) campus (WBRC, Nov 2025), and are recorded as the construction and permanent jobs figures. QTS Data Centers is owned by Blackstone (2021 take-private). Status: Bessemer approved land-use rezonings for this campus in November 2025 and again (914 acres) in April 2026, which, if a rezoning approval is treated as permitted, could argue for permitted rather than proposed. Status is kept at proposed because the cited source dated 2026-07-02 postdates both rezonings and still describes the campus as proposed, and no building permit or site-preparation start was found in any cited source.

approval_context.text: Strong and ongoing opposition. Public Facebook group 'Bessemer Data Center - We Say No!' grew to 720+ members. NAACP cited environmental justice concerns for majority-minority Bessemer community. Black Warrior Riverkeeper (BWR) and Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) opposed construction over fossil fuel and water impacts. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service raised concerns. Rezoning lawsuit filed in Jefferson County Circuit Court (temporarily enjoined; later dismissed). Bessemer City Council approved initial rezoning 5-2 in November 2025 despite crowd opposition (Councilman King and Councilwoman Thigpen dissented). 914-acre expansion rezoning approved April 2026. Some elected officials operated under NDAs with the developer prior to QTS confirmation. Homeowners filed additional lawsuits against the project.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: QTS committed to a closed-loop cooling system that does not consume water for cooling once operational. Opposition groups including Black Warrior Riverkeeper raised concerns about water impacts during construction and operation, citing proximity to a Black Warrior River tributary. Tuscaloosa County flagged for potential irreversible water impacts.

status_history.note: Project Marvel first surfaced March 2025; unnamed developer (via Logistics Land Investment LLC, an affiliate of Atlanta-based TPA Group) sought rezoning of ~700 acres in Bessemer for hyperscale data center
Bessemer City Council voted 5-2 to approve rezoning ~700 acres from agricultural (A-1) to light industrial (I-1) on November 18, 2025; developer identity still not publicly disclosed

Bessemer City Council approved rezoning of 914 additional acres in April 2026, expanding total site to ~1,607 acres; 18-building count unchanged, additional land used for wider buffers and layout flexibility
QTS Data Centers (Blackstone) publicly confirmed as operator behind Project Marvel, July 1-2, 2026; project described as in active planning stage

notes: Proposed 15-million-sq-ft, 1,218-acre campus on former citrus land east of Minute Maid Road near Orange Avenue (SR 68), Fort Pierce. St. Lucie's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-2 against recommending approval in late 2025; the applicant voluntarily withdrew the application on February 26, 2026, which a county commissioner attributed to anticipation of state AI/data-center legislation then advancing in Tallahassee (enacted as SB 484, effective July 1, 2026). Developer identity was not publicly disclosed in either source consulted as of September 2026. Coordinates corrected 2026-09-10: an earlier draft of this record and of Willow Lakes Data Center (West Midway Road) shared one pin (27.4467, -80.3256) that matched neither described parcel. This pin is derived by geocoding the landmarks the sources name — OpenStreetMap places the Minute Maid Road / Orange Avenue (SR 68) intersection at 27.44805, -80.55996, and the county description puts the site on the east side of Minute Maid Road about 2,600 ft north of that intersection, south and east of the SFWMD C-25 Canal; hence the pin is approximate rather than a confirmed parcel. On the $13.5bn figure: the applicant's notice described it as an initial capital commitment for the first 1,000 MW of capacity, not the cost of the full 15-million-sq-ft buildout. It is independently corroborated in sworn testimony before the Florida PSC, where FEIA's expert economist Dr. Fletcher Mangum projected that 'a single 1000 MW hyperscale data center campus in St. Lucie County would be expected to deliver: (i) $13.5 billion in total private capital investment over course of development' (Tr. 3423-24). Note that PSC figure is the output of an economic-impact model for a generic 1,000 MW St. Lucie campus, so it corroborates the magnitude rather than constituting an independent measurement of this project.

records.water_notes: Serverfarm's own campus page describes 'ACC Waterless' cooling in which 'cooling fluid circulates through a sealed loop' that 'recirculates water, significantly reducing water consumption' (stated as roughly 70% less than traditional cooling). status_history.note: Serverfarm affiliate SF ARK1 LLC acquired two parcels totaling 135 acres just north of Clarksville's water treatment plant on Palmer Road; land was rezoned from rural to industrial. Five buildings in three phases were then planned, with the tenant company undisclosed.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Also known as the Lancium Clean Campus. Lancium announced the site in December 2021 as a Clean Compute Campus that would host Bitcoin mining and other energy-intensive applications; Crusoe has since built an eight-building AI campus on it. Oracle gives the campus as 1,100 acres; the 2021 announcement gave about 800. Epoch AI describes the AI chips as owned by Oracle and used by OpenAI. Taylor Central Appraisal District's 2026 roll (Texas appraises property as of 1 January) lists Lancium entities as owners of the land, buildings and campus substations; Crusoe-managed entities as owners of each building's "MEP" accounts; and Oracle America as owner of computer equipment for "BUILDING 1 & 2" only, valued at $3.43 billion. Business Insider reported in July 2025 that Crusoe "has committed to spending up to $3.5 billion to build the data center site in exchange for its property tax abatement"; that is a commitment under the abatement agreements, not a reported project cost, so no investment figure is recorded here. Crusoe, Blue Owl Capital and Primary Digital Infrastructure describe the campus as funded by a "$15 billion joint-venture" (May 2025); the release does not split the figure into debt and equity or state a total project cost. Newmark said it arranged a $7.1 billion construction loan, led by JP Morgan, for the second phase. Crusoe gives the eight buildings "a total power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts"; Oracle describes its 618 MW for six buildings as "75% of total capacity", without saying what kind of capacity; Epoch AI projects 843 MW of IT power for the campus by Q4 2026. The operational capacity shown is Oracle's figure for capacity "delivered to the customer" as of 2026-09-10. Oracle did not say whether it is IT load, and "delivered" is Oracle's word, not an observation of running hardware. Crusoe expected the second phase to finish in mid-2026 (March 2025) and later "by the end of 2026" (March 2026). A separate 900 MW Crusoe campus for Microsoft (two buildings and an onsite power plant, the first building expected to be energized in mid-2027) is being built on adjacent land and is not part of this record; Epoch AI reported in April 2026 that OpenAI had reversed plans to expand this site. Construction-workforce figures conflict widely across sources and are not repeated here. Coordinates are the approximate centre of the eight data halls outlined on Epoch AI's satellite map of the campus (retrieved 2026-10-16).

approval_context.text: Abilene City Council unanimously approved the abatement; Taylor County sought additional citizen input before finalizing. Residents raised concerns about energy reliability and possible groundwater contamination, and an opposition group (saveabilene.com) formed, alongside broad local economic support. The abatement contractually requires 357 permanent jobs at a minimum $57,600 salary.
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

records.water_notes: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling with a zero-water-evaporation closed-loop system (per Measured AI, ~12,625 gallons per building per year). Mayor stated the facility would use less than 1% of Abilene's daily water. No daily water-use figure is recorded — only per-building annual volume disclosed.

status_history.note: Lancium, Taylor County and the City of Abilene announce Lancium's Clean Compute Campus on about 800 acres: $2.4 billion of planned investment over 20 years, beginning at 200 MW with expansion capacity to over 1 GW, hosting Bitcoin mining and other energy-intensive applications.
Construction of Crusoe's multi-building AI campus begins.
Announced as the flagship Stargate campus at a White House event; $500B national AI infrastructure commitment.
Crusoe begins the second phase: six more buildings, bringing the campus to eight buildings and "a total power capacity of 1.2 gigawatts", then expected to be completed in mid-2026.

Crusoe announces the campus is live: Oracle "began delivering the first NVIDIA GB200 racks in June 2025", the campus "has already begun running early training and inference workloads", and the first two buildings were energized within a year of construction starting.
Epoch AI: "Buildings 3 and 4 are estimated to be operational." The date is Epoch's estimate, allowing "another month" after a 22 April Oracle post that 200 MW was operational.

Oracle, Q4 fiscal 2026 earnings call: "Abilene, Texas today has delivered 42% of the total capacity. An additional 35% of capacity will be delivered in the next 90 days, with the remainder delivering in the subsequent quarter."

Epoch AI's latest satellite observation: buildings 5-8 are "structurally complete and roofed but not yet confirmed operational". Epoch's estimate for the campus stands at 509k H100-equivalents on 421 MW of IT power.

Oracle, Q1 fiscal 2027 earnings call: "Six of the eight campus buildings, representing 618 megawatts and 75% of total capacity, have now been delivered to the customer." Oracle did not say whether the 618 MW is IT load.

MIDA oversight provides state-level approval authority. Coordinates are approximate for western Box Elder County; exact site boundaries unpublished. Subsidies checked at the municipal tier (2026-09-05): no site-level subsidy found. Box Elder County's own Stratos Project Fact Sheet states directly: "No County funds are required to build the project. All funds will come from the developers and private investors." A May 2026 MIDA interlocal agreement covers land-use and permitting review governance (a development review committee, subdivision/site-plan requirements), not a tax-increment or abatement arrangement, and MIDA's own project-area records — which could confirm or rule out a tax-increment component — were unreachable when checked in September 2026 (mida.utah.gov redirected to an unrelated login page). Utah's EDTIF programme excludes data centres and the UCA 59-12-104 exemption is self-executing.

records.acreage_basis: Source-reported site/campus area; parcel and phase scope need verification
notes: Proposed three-building hyperscale campus at the Western New York Science, Technology and Advanced Manufacturing Park (STAMP), Town of Alabama, Genesee County - by capital investment the largest data center proposal found for New York as of September 2026. GCEDC states a "$19.46 billion" capital investment and "$285 million in PILOT/host revenues" for Genesee County, the Town of Alabama and the Oakfield-Alabama Central School District, with a public hearing "Thursday, March 19 at 7 p.m. at the Town of Alabama Fire Hall, 2230 Judge Road, Basom, NY 14013." Investigative Post reports the incentive package as "$1.46 billion in tax breaks for the creation of 125 jobs," of which "$1.43 billion in sales tax breaks" and "a $31 million mortgage tax break". The planned capacity of 500 MW records the sentence "Stream has said it will use 500 megawatts of electricity, more than 80 percent of all the power available at the STAMP industrial park" - this is stated electricity use, not a certified IT load or an interconnection award. Reported figures conflict: (a) acreage - Investigative Post says the campus spans "over 90 acres at the 1,250-acre industrial park" and the land area is set to 90; an aggregator listing gives 130 acres and had not been verified as of September 2026, so it is not used. (b) construction jobs - GCEDC's CEO is quoted at "an additional 1,000 workers temporarily," while "the agency reports on its cost-benefit analysis for the project which says construction will employ more than 16,000"; the lower, attributed figure is recorded. (c) capital cost has moved from "$6.3 billion a year ago" to "$11 billion" to "$19 billion"; the GCEDC-published $19.46B is used. As of 2026-09-09, no source retrieved states a water withdrawal volume for the campus, a confirmed hydropower allocation (the Tonawanda Seneca Nation letter opposes a prospective allocation, which is not the same as one being granted), or a construction start date - so no energy source is recorded. The AI classification is recorded as likely: the project is universally described as an AI-boom data campus but as of September 2026 no retrieved source stated the workload. Coordinates are geocoded to the Town of Alabama, Genesee County, not to a confirmed parcel. The incentive figure is a requested amount, not a confirmed or awarded PILOT; at the time of this reporting (2026-07) Gov. Hochul was considering a moratorium measure that could block it entirely. Reporting describes a requested package worth about $1.46bn from the Genesee County IDA for the STAMP site, not an awarded one. Subsidy entries have no granted-versus-requested distinction, so neither the package, its two components, nor the $285 million in PILOT/host revenues under the proposed agreements is recorded as a subsidy entry; doing so would present unawarded money as awarded. As of October 2026, none of the cited sources reports an executed IDA agreement; the Rochester Business Journal described the abatements in June 2026 as still being sought.

approval_context.text: Organized, documented opposition. The Tonawanda Seneca Nation, whose territory borders the site, wrote in April 2025 that it "strongly opposes any allocation of low-cost hydropower to a data center at STAMP"; more than 100 environmental, faith and human rights organizations plus 500 individuals statewide signed a letter opposing the project, and Stream's FIRST, smaller STAMP proposal was cancelled following a lawsuit by the Nation. The earlier proposal drew "nearly 800 written comments, 50 spoken comments made at a public hearing."
approval_context.review: source-reported local context; not a complete approval audit

status_history.note: GCEDC scheduled a public hearing on the tax-incentive package for the enlarged $19.46 billion application.

notes: Switch's second Georgia campus; distinct from its operational "The Keep" campus in Lithia Springs, Douglas County. Per DRI #4061 (submitted 2023-08-29 by the City of Cartersville): location "South of intersection of Old Alabama Rd and Bates Rd to Paulding County line within City of Cartersville"; a first phase of 126 acres with a single data center building about 1,620 ft long plus driveways, detention ponds and an electrical substation, described as 6.5% of the overall acreage; this phase targeted for Q2 2026 and the overall project for 2046; estimated build-out value $772 million and about $15 million a year in local tax revenue. Property owner per the DRI: Carter Grove (Atlanta) ASLI VI. In November 2023 the city rezoned the roughly 1,946 acres remaining in the Carter Grove Planned Development to a Technology District; the city approved a further annexation and rezoning for the campus in July 2025, with a condition barring any access, including construction access, from Etowah Ridge Trail. Bartow County's August 2026 policy statement says Switch "has not disclosed numbers, but its campus is larger than Digital Realty and its buildout could well be larger," that Switch has not forecast jobs, and that the county has granted no tax abatements or payment-in-lieu-of-taxes arrangements to these facilities. Status: aggregator sites report phase 1 as operational, but no primary source confirming construction or operation was found, so the record stays at the November 2023 rezoning approval. Coordinates are the Old Alabama Road / Bates Road intersection from OpenStreetMap, the reference point the DRI gives; the campus lies south of it.

approval_context.text: Some residents objected at the rezoning stages. In November 2023, resident Vicki Cox wrote to the city planner opposing the Technology District rezoning, citing power outages, noise, environmental impact and traffic. At the July 2025 annexation and rezoning, residents raised concerns about access from Etowah Ridge Trail, and the approval barred it. No organized opposition campaign against the Switch campus was found.

Total campus target: 1.8M sq ft, 320 MW, ~$5B investment across all phases. Phase 1 (225,000 sq ft white space) and Phase 2 (312,000 sq ft) operational; Phase 3 in planning/early construction as of 2025. Michigan's largest data center by capacity. approval_context.text: The project repurposed the long-vacant, iconic Steelcase 'Pyramid' and is broadly welcomed locally, with the township receiving roughly $430K/year from Switch and its tenants. notes: 500MW on-site gas-fired data center campus (~200-600 acre portion of a larger ~600-acre Tooele Valley Public Infrastructure District development that also includes a truck stop, hotel, and warehouses near I-80); backed by Utah Inland Port Authority financing. Developer plans a reverse-osmosis plant discharging ~250,000 gallons/day of brine into Great Salt Lake wetlands, drawing significant local opposition. Subsidies checked (2026-09-08): no site-level subsidy confirmed for this parcel. A $4.875M Utah Inland Port Authority Infrastructure Bank loan was reported in April 2024 to Zenith Bolinder, LLC — the Delaware LLC that petitioned UIPA in March 2024 to create the Tooele Valley Public Infrastructure District, representing 100% of surface property owners within it, and which KSL describes as "a partnership with longtime Utah developer Zenith Development"; Charles Akerlow appears both as the petition's contact sponsor and as Zenith Development's managing director. The two are affiliated but are not the same legal entity, the loan terms were not confirmed against a primary document, and the district's boundary exhibit is a scanned image that could not be read — so whether that loan reaches this data-centre parcel is unresolved. UIPA's executive director stated in July 2026 that the authority's involvement covers transportation within a 600-acre portion and does not extend to the southern section planned for the data centre.

status_history.note: Public hearing held on a state water-discharge permit (UPDES UT0026409) required for the project; permit still pending as of the hearing.

notes: Redevelopment of the former Remington Arms firearms plant, which ceased production in 2024. WKTV: "Turin Hoefler Avenue LLC submitted a revised application" to the NYSDEC "Brownfield Cleanup Program" in January 2026 for "Site C," a "7.837-acre parcel," with a "250,000-square-foot AI data center" as the intended post-remediation use, at "14 Hoefler Ave., Ilion, NY"; the site has "widespread contamination in the soil, especially with heavy metals like arsenic, lead, and copper at levels above state cleanup standards for commercial use" and "15 vacant industrial buildings dating to the early 1900s," and the developer describes it as a "fossil-fuel-free, 100% electric site." The planned capacity of 200 MW comes from the Rockefeller Institute of Government's tracker entry for the project ("200 MW"), not from WKTV, which states no MW figure. County discrepancy: WKTV's article says Oneida County; the Rockefeller Institute says "Village of Ilion, Herkimer County." Ilion is in Herkimer County, so Herkimer is recorded and the WKTV attribution is treated as an error. The 7.837-acre figure is the Brownfield Site C parcel only; trade press describes a larger ~32-acre overall plant site and two 250,000 sq ft buildings, neither of which had been verified against a cited source as of September 2026, so neither is recorded. No permanent-jobs figure is recorded: the source says only that the project "aims to exceed the 274 positions lost when Remington closed," which is an aspiration, not a count. As of 2026-09-09, neither cited source states an investment figure, water/cooling detail, utility, or IDA or PILOT agreement. Ivey in 2023, but states no dollar totals for either. Acreage (~50 acres) and the exact street address/postal code are corroborated only via a single aggregator/cached-search path (Data Center Dynamics coverage of the site's HSBC/Capital One former-tenant history could not be retrieved), so they are single-path and not independently cross-verified; treat address/acreage as approximate. Former site occupant: HSBC (built ~2007), later Capital One (acquired HSBC's US card operations, 2012), vacant and auctioned ~2023 before Chirisa's redevelopment. As of August 2026, no SEC filing or Bloom Energy investor press release had been located to corroborate, and neither is cited as a source. methodology.counting: Named facility, building and campus/project inventory records across the 50 states and DC. Unnamed objects, standalone generation and standalone crypto mines are excluded. Counts do not certify unique parcels or operating buildings; campuses can contain several buildings.
methodology.deduplication: Exact normalized facility names in the same state within 1 km are consolidated. Current-source additions sharing an OSM object, operator and location are also consolidated. Every merged ID remains as an alias. Different named buildings are not fabricated from campus totals. Ambiguous parent/child relationships require review.
methodology.classification: Hyperscale / cloud is an operator-based classification for Amazon/AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. Other records are classified smaller below 50 reported MW or large at 50 MW and above. The 50 MW cutoff is a Syncranicity screening convention, not an industry definition. Unknown capacity is never classified as small.
methodology.power: MW is reported data-center capacity or electrical demand, not necessarily metered usage. Basis and project phase are retained. Generation-only capacity is listed as power-supply context and is excluded from data-center capacity and size classification. No MW is inferred from acres or floor area; overlapping phases are not summed.
methodology.acreage: Source-reported land area is retained with its scope. Independent reviews may use official parcel land area, with explicit unit conversion. Building square feet are never converted to land acres. Purchased-acre history remains on separate acquisition events.
methodology.limitations: This is a sourced but incomplete inventory, not a complete U.S. census or completed deed/permit audit. Current-source community notes are labeled source-reported local context. Original purchaser, title chain, historical listing, price and final approval conditions remain unresolved for most records. The source may contain stale or incorrect facts. Do not treat this as a completed training dataset of successful projects.
